articles.title: Google's work in schools aims to create a 'pipeline of future users,' internal documents say
articles.summary: Newly filed internal documents show how Google viewed its work with schools as a way of turning children into lifelong customers — while the company simultaneously acknowledged research suggesting that YouTube, one of Google’s main platforms, can be unsafe and distracting.
articles.body: Newly filed internal documents show how Google viewed its work with schools as a way of turning children into lifelong customers — while the company simultaneously acknowledged research suggesting that YouTube, one of Google’s main platforms, can be unsafe and distracting. In a 2018 presentation, one slide noted that the public sees YouTube as problematic for students because there is “No way to block unsafe content, comments, ads,” a challenge without a workable solution. A presentation last updated in 2024 said some survey respondents blamed YouTube for keeping them awake at night, among other negative effects on their well-being. At the same time, other presentations described how Google’s growing presence in schools — through Chromebooks as well as its learning platforms and YouTube — helped the company build a “Pipeline of future users.” One internal November 2020 presentation slide said acclimating children to Google’s ecosystem in school would hopefully lead them to use its products as adults: “You get that loyalty early, and potentially for life.” Another undated slide deck suggested imagining a world where “Parents ask their children ‘Why aren’t you watching more YouTube?’” and “School Administrators shift budgets from Textbooks to YouTube subscriptions.” Education experts and parent advocates who are concerned about schools overusing devices for instruction said the documents shed new light, in candid detail, on the business motivations behind one of the biggest technology companies marketing its products to teachers and school administrators. “It just proves the kind of fear that we’ve all had,” said Jared Cooney Horvath, a cognitive neuroscientist and education consultant who recently wrote a book criticizing technology in schools. “These companies speak about learning, but to them, learning is just the cover they’re using for these practices of ‘How do we get customers now’ and ‘How do we keep them for life.’” Do you have a story to share about technology in education? Contact reporter Tyler Kingkade The internal Google records, which were heavily redacted, were filed by plaintiffs Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California as part of a major lawsuit in which families, school districts and state attorneys general are suing several technology giants — Meta, ByteDance, Snap and Google — claiming that the corporations purposely marketed addictive and damaging social media to children. Snap settled its portion of the suit this week, on undisclosed terms, as the other companies move closer to trial over questions of whether they were obligated to warn schools of their platforms’ negative effects or to implement more restrictions for young users. The companies have broadly argued that the plaintiffs are inaccurately describing their products, blaming them for harm they did not cause and incorrectly seeking to hold them accountable for content created by users, which they are protected against under a law commonly referred to as Section 230. Hundreds of school districts joined the litigation, but a judge chose six last year to proceed to trial first. A Kentucky district will be the first school system to go to trial in June. Google didn’t answer questions from NBC News about the purpose and audience of the internal documents that were included in court filings, but Jack Malon, a Google spokesperson, said in an email that the “documents mischaracterize our work.” Malon added that while the company does not directly market YouTube to schools, "we have responded to meet the strong demand from educators for high-quality, curriculum-aligned content. Administrators maintain full control over platform usage and schools must obtain parental consent before granting access to students under 18." Sarah Gardner, CEO of Heat Initiative, a parent activist group critical of social media platforms, found the newly released Google files alarming. She wants to see schools and political leaders put more guardrails on technology in classrooms to ensure that the products benefit students. “These documents confirm that suspicion that there are ulterior motives to companies pushing technology into classrooms,” Gardner said. “And so we need to be asking why we’re letting them do that.” When schools began installing bulky desktop personal computers in the 1990s, they mostly bought Apple products, taking advantage of discounts the company offered. While Microsoft Windows gained ground in the 2000s, schools shifted toward Google after it debuted the Chromebook in 2011, and the company has dominated the education computer hardware market for the past decade. Schools now account for 80% of all purchases of Chromebooks, according to market research firms. Google said in 2017 that more than half of all American public school children use Google applications and products for classwork and stated in 2021 that over 170 million students and teachers worldwide use them. Schools also use YouTube, with varying restrictions. Some give students and teachers free rein, while others block it entirely. Teachers can embed YouTube videos in course content through Google’s specialized education platform. Google requires students to have parental permission to access YouTube on school devices. “Insofar as we are looking at how teachers are engaging with YouTube content, we are trying to make it easier for them to do it,” Kathryn Kurtz, global head of youth and learning at YouTube, said in a March 2025 deposition that was partially unredacted this week. “And one of the things that we heard is that teachers wanted to be able to show YouTube video even if their school had made the determination that they wanted to block access to YouTube.” Google has argued in recent court filings that YouTube can’t be that much of a problem for the school districts suing because they still use it to communicate with families and they allow students and teachers to use it on campus. The internal Google documents were made public several days after a U.S. Senate hearing on concerns about the overuse of technology in public schools. Horvath, the neuroscientist, and three other witnesses argued that school-issued laptops and tablets can distract children and that schools too frequently use unproven digital tools when research shows analog ways of learning are more effective. Ahead of the hearing, the two largest teachers unions, the American Library Association and 14 education trade groups wrote a letter defending education technology and urging federal lawmakers not to restrict students’ access or screen time. Stacy Hawthorne, board chair of the Consortium for School Networking, an association for school technology officials that signed the letter, is concerned that some are conflating social media, which can cause problems for children, with technology more broadly, which can help students learn. “There’s a big chasm between ‘Social media is bad for kids’ and ‘We need to pull computers out of schools,’” she said. Kurtz, from YouTube, said in her deposition that the company had not measured the effectiveness of YouTube to improve students’ learning and did not have data to show its content boosted students’ grades, graduation rates or test scores. One internal Google presentation, which is undated, conceded that using YouTube for learning is hard because the platform is distracting and disorganized. It showed an example in which YouTube recommended “Will Ferrell Hilarious Acceptance Speech” from user “cocksandballs123” to someone who had searched for content about “linear equations.” Justin Reich, an associate professor of digital media at MIT and the director of the university’s Teaching Systems Lab, said YouTube is caught between tailoring its product to schools and appealing to a vast global audience. “There’s no capitalist way to win by making your product less engaging,” he said.

articles.title: Nuvem de andorinhas em Cuiabá: biólogo explica rota das aves | G1
articles.standfirst: Aves fugiram do inverno na América do Norte e usam a capital como parada para descanso e alimentação.
articles.summary: Aves fugiram do inverno na América do Norte e usam a capital como parada para descanso e alimentação.
articles.body:
O biólogo e professor da Universidade Federal de Mato Grosso (UFMT), Vítor de Queiroz Piacentini , explicou por que milhares de andorinhas se reúnem todas as tardes em um condomínio no Jardim Tropical , em Cuiabá . As aves fazem parte de um processo migratório e, além de chamarem a atenção pelos voos sincronizados antes de pousar em árvores e fios para passar a noite , ajudam a reduzir a quantidade de insetos no ambiente, incluindo mosquitos que podem transmitir doenças.

À TV Centro América, o especialista destacou que as aves migram todos os anos da América do Norte para fugir do inverno no Hemisfério Norte . No Brasil, a maioria se concentra na região amazônica, mas alguns grupos avançam até o Brasil Central.

“Não tem como a gente saber ao certo quanto tempo elas vão ficar. O comum é que os indivíduos acabem ficando não a estação de invernada inteira no mesmo local, mas que eles se dispersem em função da disponibilidade de alimento”, explicou.

Segundo o biólogo, as aves podem permanecer na região por algumas semanas ou até poucos meses . A tendência é que o grupo se divida gradualmente e parte dos indivíduos procure outros locais para descansar e se alimentar.

O período de permanência das andorinhas na América do Sul costuma ocorrer entre outubro e fevereiro ou março, podendo se estender até abril para alguns indivíduos . Nesse intervalo, elas podem percorrer diferentes áreas antes de iniciar o retorno à América do Norte.

Em abril, por exemplo, é comum que as aves se concentrem em regiões mais ao norte da Amazônia, como nas proximidades de Manaus. Piacentini explica que a migração exige bastante energia e, por isso, as aves fazem paradas durante o percurso para descansar e se alimentar antes de continuar a viagem.

“Nem sempre elas conseguem fazer toda a rota de uma vez só. Muitas vezes, os indivíduos fazem paradas de descanso para se alimentar, para, entre aspas, se reabastecer para continuar a jornada”, disse.

Por isso, ainda não é possível afirmar se o grupo que aparece diariamente no Jardim Tropical já escolheu o local como ponto de permanência temporária ou se está apenas fazendo uma parada durante o deslocamento.

Nuvem de aves migratórias chega a condomínio no Jardim Tropical, em Cuiabá. — Foto: Giovanna Baiocco/g1 MT

Além do espetáculo visual, a presença das andorinhas pode trazer benefícios ambientais. Segundo o professor, cada ave consome centenas ou até milhares de insetos ao longo do dia, contribuindo para reduzir a quantidade desses animais no ambiente.

“Você pode imaginar o quanto um bando numeroso desses, que deve ter alguns milhares de indivíduos de andorinhas, retira de insetos do ambiente ao redor, o que pode ser inclusive benéfico se a gente pensar em mosquitos transmissores de doenças”, afirmou.

O biólogo destaca que as aves também contribuem para os chamados serviços ecossistêmicos, ou seja, benefícios que os animais oferecem ao equilíbrio ambiental e à vida humana. Ele ressalta ainda que as andorinhas são consideradas espécies nativas do Brasil, por passarem parte do ciclo de vida no país, e são protegidas pela legislação ambiental.

As andorinhas e seus ninhos são protegidos pela Lei de Crimes Ambientais (Lei nº 9.605/1998) e pela Lei de Proteção à Fauna (Lei nº 5.197/1967). A legislação proíbe, sem autorização, a captura de aves silvestres e a destruição de ninhos e abrigos naturais, com previsão de penalidades para os responsáveis.

Milhares de andorinhas fazem parada temporária durante rota migratória, segundo especilista — Foto: Giovanna Baiocco/ g1 MT

Em nota, a Secretaria Municipal de Meio Ambiente e Desenvolvimento Urbano (SMADES) orienta os moradores a não capturar, tocar ou afugentar as aves, nem interferir em seus ninhos.

Caso seja necessário realizar algum tipo de manejo, captura ou remoção, o procedimento deve ser avaliado e conduzido pelos órgãos ambientais competentes, como o Instituto Brasileiro do Meio Ambiente e dos Recursos Naturais Renováveis (Ibama), conforme as autorizações aplicáveis.

articles.title: Iguá Sergipe: Paula Violante assume liderança da concessionária | G1
articles.standfirst: Diretora executiva de Operações da Iguá Saneamento passa a liderar as atividades no estado.
articles.summary: A Iguá Sergipe anunciou que Paula Violante assume interinamente a liderança da concessionária de saneamento após a saída de Fernando Vieira do cargo de diretor-geral.
articles.body:
Diretor-geral da Iguá Sergipe, Fernando Vieira. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Sergipe

Fernando Vieira deixou o cargo de diretor-geral da Iguá Sergipe nesta segunda-feira (19). A mudança na gestão da concessionária de saneamento foi comunicada pela empresa por meio de nota oficial.

Com a saída do executivo, a liderança da operação no estado passa a ser exercida interinamente por Paula Violante, que ocupa a diretoria executiva de Operações da Iguá Saneamento.

Segundo a companhia, a transição garante a continuidade das atividades e dos compromissos assumidos em Sergipe.

O motivo da alteração na liderança da concessionária não foi informado.

articles.title: Prefeitura de Poços de Caldas atrasa repasses a instituições; Apae alerta para risco aos atendimentos | G1
articles.standfirst: Entidade afirma que recursos municipais correspondem a mais de 50% da manutenção dos serviços pactuados. Prefeitura confirmou atraso de um mês e meio e informou que trabalha para regularizar os pagamentos.
articles.summary: Entidade afirma que recursos municipais correspondem a mais de 50% da manutenção dos serviços pactuados. Prefeitura confirmou atraso de um mês e meio e informou que trabalha para regularizar os pagamentos.
articles.body:
A Prefeitura de Poços de Caldas (MG) atrasou o repasse de recursos destinados a instituições assistenciais do município. Na Apae, que atende quase mil pessoas, os valores transferidos pelo Executivo representam cerca de metade de toda a arrecadação e são utilizados na manutenção dos atendimentos.

Segundo a diretora institucional da Apae, Gláucia Boaretto, os recursos são fundamentais para a continuidade dos serviços pactuados.

“Acho que, para todas as entidades, ele é de suma importância. Ele não é a totalidade, mas ultrapassa a casa de 50% da manutenção dos serviços que são pactuados. Então, havendo atraso, gera um desconforto e uma insegurança no cumprimento das ações”, afirmou.

Prefeitura de Poços de Caldas atrasa repasses a instituições; Apae alerta para risco aos atendimentos — Foto: Reprodução EPTV

Os atrasos podem comprometer os atendimentos. Para evitar que a situação se agrave, a instituição deve reunir-se nesta semana com o Conselho Municipal da Criança e do Adolescente e com a Prefeitura.

“Para garantir que a gente não pare os trabalhos, que continue a prestar um serviço de qualidade. Mas estamos ainda em negociação, em articulação, para definir qual é a melhor decisão a ser tomada, e também aguardando uma posição do nosso Executivo”, disse a diretora.

Em Poços de Caldas, 58 instituições possuem termo de colaboração com a Prefeitura e executam diferentes tipos de serviços. No ano passado, os repasses chegaram a R$ 26,5 milhões.

Até 23 de setembro deste ano, foram transferidos R$ 12,8 milhões. Relatos de que os atrasos já estariam a afetar os serviços chegaram à Câmara Municipal.

“A Câmara vem acompanhando a situação com muita preocupação. São diversos os relatos das instituições e de funcionários dessas instituições, além da preocupação com a população atendida. A gente vem acompanhando todo este tipo de reclamação, que já está a começar a afetar diretamente o serviço prestado à nossa população”, afirmou o vereador Flávio Togni de Lima e Silva (MDB).

Prefeitura de Poços de Caldas atrasa repasses a instituições; Apae alerta para risco aos atendimentos — Foto: Reprodução / EPTV

A Câmara chegou a oferecer a antecipação dos valores que são devolvidos pelo Legislativo no final do ano, para que os repasses fossem regularizados. Sem retorno, foi enviado um ofício ao Ministério Público para que sejam tomadas medidas. O documento é assinado por seis vereadores.

“A gente estima que é uma dívida alta, considerável, que afeta todas as nossas instituições, como eu já disse, os funcionários dessas instituições e a população de Poços de Caldas que é atendida por esses servidores”, disse o vereador.

Nenhum representante da prefeitura quis conceder entrevista. Por meio de nota enviada pela assessoria de comunicação, o Executivo informou que, nesta segunda-feira, efetuou parte dos pagamentos referentes aos meses de julho e agosto.

A Prefeitura confirmou que os atrasos continuam, mas afirmou que agora correspondem a um mês e meio. Informou ainda que nenhum serviço foi interrompido e reforçou que segue empenhada na regularização dos pagamentos, assegurando a manutenção dos serviços socioassistenciais no município.

articles.title: Carros de luxo e aviões em evento em Goiás valem R$ 1 bilhão | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo o organizador Renato Peixoto, entre os carros mais caros no evento estavam Lamborghini Reventón, avaliado em R$ 8 milhões, e a Ferrari Purossangue, de R$ 8 milhões.
articles.summary: Com modelos como Lamborghini e Ferrari, evento de carros de luxo em Goiânia reuniu frota bilionária e arrecadou alimentos para doação.
articles.body:
Os aviões e carros de luxo que chamaram atenção durante encontro em Goiânia valem juntos quase R$ 1 bilhão, informou um dos organizadores do evento, Renato Peixoto. Foram mais de 160 veículos que “desfilaram” por quase 50 quilômetros, partindo do Shopping Flamboyant, no Jardim Goiás, na capital, em direção ao Aeródromo Condomínio Liberty, em Goianápolis ( veja acima ).

O evento aconteceu neste sábado (17). Segundo o organizador, entre os carros mais caros no evento estavam Lamborghini Reventón, avaliado em R$ 8 milhões, e a Ferrari Purossangue, de R$ 8 milhões. Além dos carros, o evento reuniu aviões cujos valores variam entre 2 e 6 milhões de dólares.

“É um evento que reúne empresários, proprietários de carros esportivos, para curtirem o carro e se encontrarem com pessoas que têm a mesma paixão. O evento The Next Level, no Libert, foi onde a gente juntou os proprietários de carros esportivos com proprietários de aeronaves, de helicópteros e de aviões, para conectar os dois mundos”, explicou Renato.

Carros de luxo formam fila e impressionam em Goiânia, Goiás — Foto: Reprodução/Pedro Molinari

Além de Renato, o evento também contou com apoio de Pedro Molinari, Lucas Bizinoto e Samuel Ivanaskas e arrecadou alimentos não perecíveis entre os participantes. Eles serão doados a moradores de bairros carentes de Goiânia e Aparecida de Goiânia.

“O objetivo é unir amantes e donos de carros de luxo, em um evento beneficente com doação de alimentos e também network”, explicou Samuel Ivanaskas.

articles.title: O líder de seita apocalíptica que deixou quase 200 crianças morrerem | G1
articles.standfirst: O autoproclamado pastor Paul Mackenzie foi considerado culpado pela morte de 191 pessoas. Destas, todas, exceto uma, eram crianças.
articles.summary: O autoproclamado pastor Paul Mackenzie foi considerado culpado pela morte de 191 pessoas. Destas, todas, exceto uma, eram crianças.
articles.body:
Importante: esta reportagem contém detalhes que podem ser perturbadores para alguns leitores.

O líder de uma seita apocalíptica queniana, Paul Mackenzie, foi considerado culpado pelo assassinato de 191 pessoas. Todas elas, exceto uma, eram crianças.

Mackenzie ordenou que os membros da sua seita deixassem seus filhos passarem fome até a morte, para poderem "encontrar Jesus".

Sua doutrina proibia a educação e afirmava que a medicina moderna era "maligna".

Outros 28 líderes da seita também foram condenados por assassinato. Todos eles haviam se declarado inocentes e defenderam repetidamente que ninguém havia sido forçado a morrer.

Ao emitir seu julgamento por oito horas na cidade portuária de Mombasa, no Quênia , a juíza Diana Mochache afirmou que os seguidores de Mackenzie acreditavam que ele fosse "porta-voz de Jesus".

Um dos acusados declarou que Mackenzie havia dito aos seus seguidores que qualquer pessoa que "resistisse à ordem de jejuar deveria ser forçada a ir para o céu com socos e pontapés".

Os sepultamentos no interior da floresta onde ficava a seita eram chamados de "casamentos". Os mortos "eram homenageados como tendo se casado com Jesus", segundo a juíza.

Uma testemunha declarou que uma mulher grávida havia sido proibida de amamentar seu bebê recém-nascido, que morreu 12 dias depois. "Ela foi instruída a jejuar até a morte e seguir seus filhos", segundo a testemunha.

O ex-chefe de segurança de Mackenzie, Enos Amanya Ngala, foi inicialmente acusado, mas fez um acordo de confissão e se tornou testemunha da promotoria.

Mackenzie e outros líderes da seita também enfrentam vários outros processos judiciais, que incluem acusações de terrorismo, radicalização e negação de educação a crianças.

Mas esta é a primeira vez em que o pastor enfrentou o veredito pelas acusações mais sérias de assassinato. Ele deve receber sua sentença no dia 6 de novembro.

Paul Mackenzie, líder de culto no Quênia, comparece ao tribunal — Foto: REUTERS/Stringer

Mackenzie foi preso em 2023, após a descoberta de mais de 400 corpos em covas rasas na floresta de Shakahola, perto do litoral queniano, onde ele liderava seus seguidores vindos de todo o país.

Stephen Mwiti tem 48 anos. Ele conta que perdeu todos os seus seis filhos para a seita. Sua ex-esposa também foi condenada por assassinato, além de Mackenzie.

"Sou um homem feliz por todas as pessoas terem sido condenadas", contou ele à BBC, fora do tribunal.

"Todos os meus seis filhos morreram na floresta de Shakahola", declarou Mwiti antes do veredito. Visivelmente emocionado, ele segurava uma fotografia da sua família. "Só encontrei e enterrei os restos do meu filho Samuel.

Foram contratados 17 homens da cidade próxima para a terrível tarefa de escavar as covas rasas. Alguns deles receberam apenas US$ 8 (cerca de R$ 40) por dia.

"Cada cova que encontrávamos tinha pelo menos três corpos", conta James, um dos escavadores. "Alguns dos restos eram de crianças com poucas semanas de idade."

"Certa vez, encontramos 12 corpos de crianças enfileirados dentro de uma cova. Era enorme, os corpos estavam dispostos como se fossem roupas, um em cima do outro."

Os escavadores descreveram alguns dos corpos das crianças como tendo suas "mãos e pés amarrados e os corpos enrolados em lençóis".

Mais de 400 corpos foram desenterrados na floresta de Shakahola, no leste do Quênia — Foto: AFP via Getty Images

Muitos dos seguidores de Mackenzie eram de outras partes do Quênia , mas alguns dos restos são de pessoas conhecidas da comunidade. O motivo é que os membros da seita, muitas vezes, visitavam a cidade próxima de Shakahola em busca de mantimentos e água do rio Galana, que atravessa o local.

"Às vezes, carregávamos pessoas na motocicleta em direção à floresta", conta outro escavador, Salim Karisa. "Mas era tão secreto e planejado que ninguém sabia dizer o que acontecia lá dentro."

Mackenzie fundou os Ministérios Internacionais da Boa Nova em 2003. Nos 16 anos seguintes, a popularidade da igreja aumentou, atraindo milhares de seguidores nas suas filiais por todo o Quênia .

Sua igreja mantinha uma estação de televisão chamada Times TV. Ela transmitia seus sermões, da sua igreja em Malindi, no sudeste do país.

Seus sermões dos Dias Finais incluíam teorias da conspiração que descreviam a educação como "maligna", a assistência médica como "contra a doutrina" e os documentos de identidade digitais como "marca do demônio".

O filho de Paul Mackenzie, Dan Paul Mackenzie, afirmou ter trabalhado como câmera na igreja. "As crianças se sentavam atrás, os adultos no meio e todos cantavam canções de louvor a manhã inteira", descreve ele.

O autoproclamado pastor começava seus ardentes sermões ao meio-dia. Alguns deles incluíam a "expulsão de demônios".

A igreja principal fechou em 2019 e Paul Mackenzie se mudou para a floresta de Shakahola, incentivando seus fiéis a segui-lo.

Peter Shukrani tem 23 anos. Ele conta que sua mãe se mudou para Shakahola com ele naquela época.

Ele começou a frequentar a igreja de Mackenzie quando tinha oito anos de idade e o descreve como seu "pai espiritual". Ele destaca que "nunca fala mal dele".

Na floresta, Shukrani ficou doente e sua condição se deteriorou porque as medicações eram proibidas.

"Minha mãe jogava fora todos os remédios que eu deveria tomar porque ela acreditava que apenas Deus poderia me curar", relembra Shukrani.

A comunidade foi descrita como composta por casas de barro espalhadas pela vasta floresta.

"Vivíamos uma vida normal, calma, jejuando por alguns dias e, depois, tendo uma pequena refeição", ele conta.

Os criadores de animais da região descobriram os primeiros restos mortais em março de 2023. Àquela altura, centenas de pessoas haviam morrido.

"Nós carregávamos alguns para fora da floresta, mas eles eram tão frágeis que morriam nos nossos braços", explica Salim Karisa, um dos escavadores.

Shukrani foi um dos homens resgatados da floresta. Ele estava doente e acamado há semanas, mas sua condição havia se agravado porque sua mãe jogava fora todas as medicações necessárias para sua recuperação.

"Minha mãe acreditava na doutrina do pastor Mackenzie, de que a medicina era maligna", explica ele. "Eu teria morrido se não tivesse sido resgatado da floresta de Shakahola."

Muitos dos corpos ainda não foram identificados, devido ao seu avançado estado de decomposição.

Nos documentos judiciais, vários deles são indicados como "meninos desconhecidos" e identificados pela localização do seu túmulo e data da descoberta.

Os seguidores de Paul Mackenzie acreditavam que ele fosse o 'porta-voz de Jesus', segundo o juiz — Foto: AFP via Getty Images

Mesmo com o sofrimento imposto aos seguidores de Mackenzie — homens, mulheres e crianças que morreram de fome, estrangulamento ou foram espancados até a morte —, sem falar no seu próprio sofrimento, Shukrani acredita que Mackenzie é "uma pessoa boa, que se importa comigo".

"Mackenzie não forçou ninguém a jejuar. As pessoas fizeram estas escolhas por si próprias devido às suas crenças", declarou ele, antes do anúncio do veredito.

"Eu ainda o amo e ele continua sendo meu pastor."

Já Dan Mackenzie acreditava que seu pai deveria ser considerado culpado de assassinato.

"Ele foi o líder, ele era alguém que eles procuravam. Por isso, ele é um assassino em massa", declarou ele, antes do veredito.

articles.title: 'Give us lessons on personal finance and how to get a job,' teens say
articles.summary: Teenagers say they want more work experience at school and opportunities to improve their communication skills.
articles.body:
More than four in 10 UK teenagers want more work experience opportunities at school, with a similar proportion calling for more guidance on how to apply for jobs, a survey for the BBC suggests.

The online survey, by Survation, asked 2,000 young people aged 13 to 18 about the world of work and the help they need to secure employment once they leave full-time education.

Some called for more support with their communications skills and raised concerns about stress management and personal finances.

Skills Minister Jacqui Smith said it was the government's "mission" to ensure teenagers leave school "confident about their next step and equipped with the skills and experience they need to succeed".

In England, the government wants to guarantee two weeks' of work experience for every young person during secondary school.

It's an opportunity not all teenagers are currently given, the survey for the BBC suggests, with more than half of respondents saying they had not done any.

When teenagers were asked in the survey what skills or guidance they would like more of at school, the most common responses were more work experience opportunities (44%) and help managing finances (43%).

Respondents said they also wanted guidance on how to apply for jobs (42%) as well as how to manage stress and mental health (39%) and develop their communication skills (38%).

As part of the Teen Summit project by Radio 5 Live and Bitesize, the BBC followed four students from Newcastle - Param, McKenzie, Jasmine and Javaris - as they tried out roles for the first time as part of their work experience placements.

"I'm terrified about the future. I feel very uncertain about it," 15-year-old Jasmine said.

Jasmine said she enjoyed her placement working on logo designs at web design and development agency Readysalted.

But she said the placement made her realise she was probably unsuited to an office job.

"Hats off to all the workers that have to do this every single day," she said.

She said it gave her a real taste of working life, but that she was still worried about making "the wrong decision" around what to do next.

"I think about exams and not getting the right grades, which leads to not getting into the right course and then not getting into university, and it's very stressful," she said. "That's always on my mind."

A 15-minute walk up the road from Jasmine's placement, near the centre of Newcastle, her classmate Param had his work experience at social housing group Re:Gen.

Param said it showed him there was more to work than simply having the right knowledge and understanding.

"Social skills are just as important as academic skills," he said, after a day of meeting clients and working with people he had never met before.

He also spent time with staff carrying out quality checks on social houses, looking for loose fittings or uneven surfaces.

"It's given us a taste of the real world," he said. "It's bringing us out of our comfort zones."

As an aspiring pilot, he said schools should not just provide work experience opportunities, but additional teaching on other aspects of adult life outside of work.

"We need to know about houses, mortgages, selling and tax," he said.

Javaris, who spent a week's placement at Siemens Energy alongside friend and classmate McKenzie, also said the work experience challenged his social skills in a new setting.

"I've really never been in a workplace with people I don't know, having to socialise and having to teach me about things I've never learned before," he said.

Javaris ultimately wants to become a doctor, but said the week had given him an insight into how different parts of a company are run.

McKenzie, who wants to study chemistry or become a firefighter, said he enjoyed speaking with people in different jobs and seeing the differences between "hands-on" roles and office work.

In light of AI and new technologies in the workplace, nearly a third of teenagers responding to the survey (32%) said they thought school was preparing them badly for the future of work - although more than half of teenagers said it was preparing them well.

One of the areas young people said they wanted more help with was developing communication skills.

The BBC set Javaris and McKenzie a challenge to help develop their own communication skills, and put some of their thoughts directly to one of their work experience company's bosses - Aaron Smith, head of business for GT Service at Siemens Energy.

So, beyond academic results, what skills are employers really looking for?

"You know, you can be extremely academically strong, but if you can't do a presentation, if you can't speak in public, if you are in a group exercise and you step back, these are the kind of softer skills that will be picked out in an apprenticeship assessment centre," Smith said.

The pair were also keen to know if they should be studying AI as part of their education.

McKenzie said he thinks AI should be added to the national curriculum, adding that "it's getting harder and harder to see what's AI and what's not".

He said he was also concerned about the impact AI may have on the availability of jobs, but added that he was "positive" about his future prospects.

"Certainly AI is huge within the industry," Smith said.

"We're actively encouraging AI training, AI learning, AI applications in our business to make us better."

The teens' deputy principal, Nigel Holmes, said while it was "really important" for schools to prepare students for their academic qualifications, "we'd be really remiss if we didn't look at those wider employability skills that I think we know are really important".

On Sunday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted the government to "invest in the success of our young people" , with plans for thousands of job opportunities expected this week.

Despite the backdrop of AI and a tough jobs market, more than three quarters of teens surveyed said they still felt positive about their futures.

In the weeks since their work experience placements, all four students have said they feel clearer about their future opportunities.

Javaris said he thinks work experience should be mandatory, and that it "really gives you an insight of what to expect [as] you get older".

For Jasmine, who prior to her placement was worried about what the future might hold, things now feel a little less uncertain.

After talking to her school careers adviser, she is considering studying psychology.

"I was kind of worried that I wouldn't get the grades I wanted. I still am a bit," she said.

"But I definitely know now that even if you don't get grade nines, you'll still have a future and you can still be happy with your job."

articles.title: Southampton trade historians teach AI to read handwriting
articles.summary: A project using data from the Elizabethan Era to the Industrial Revolution analyses trade routes.
articles.body:
Historians have uncovered 461 years of Britain's maritime past using AI.

The study involved training AI to process about 100,000 pages of handwritten records, a task that would have taken years if done manually.

The University of Southampton project revealed how Britain grew into an Empire through its links with Europe, using data spanning from the Elizabethan Era in the 16th Century, to just before the Industrial Revolution in the 18th Century.

Researchers found that key goods Britons traded included coal and ale, followed by children's toys from China, sheep guts and Venice treacle, a herbal medicine that was believed to cure almost any illness.

Historian and lead researcher Professor Craig Lambert said compiling the data, which was taken from leather-bound parchment books at the National Archives in Kew, was a "massive task" but AI "sped up the process enormously".

The AI learned how to read and recognise the historical handwriting belonging to early-modern seafarers to learn details about "who was trading what, with whom, when and where," researchers said.

It also gave insights into the maritime landscape of the past. Researchers said that Europe was once a more crucial trading partner than might have previously been thought.

The project found that even as the British Empire was expanding, between 1696–97 "European markets accounted for around 80 percent of the recorded value of England's overseas trade".

Lost towns were also discovered, along with their vanished ports.

Ravenspurn in East Yorkshire, a once-thriving trading hub, completely sunk in the North Sea after severe coastal erosion.

The project is supported by a team of specialists in maritime history, global history and computer science.

Researchers said it has mapped the development of England's trade routes and global impact over two centuries in detail for the first time.

An interactive map has been developed out of the research to help people navigate and explore the extensive data for themselves.

articles.title: US rock band Wheatus sponsor U13s football team in Worcestershire
articles.summary: The US frontman, responsible for Teenage Dirtbag, says the team could be treated to a private show.
articles.body:
An unlikely friendship has led to an even more unlikely partnership, with US rock band Wheatus sponsoring a Worcestershire youth football team.

Nunnery Wood U13s Phoenix, based in Worcester, now wear kits bearing the Teenage Dirtbag band's logo after coach Graham approached them for support.

The connection began when Graham and his son Bertie, both fans of the group, met members of Wheatus at a gig in Gloucester and stayed in touch afterwards.

"I thought Wheatus' logo would look amazing on a football shirt," Graham said, adding: "I cheekily asked if they fancied sponsoring the team, and they said yes."

Graham has been a fan of Wheatus since the band's self-titled debut album was released in 2000 and won tickets to meet the sextet at Gloucester Guildhall in 2023.

After introducing his son to their music he knew he needed to take Bertie along, however, he was too young to attend at the time.

But the band managed to pull some strings that enabled the then nine-year-old to meet his heroes.

Once the meet and greet was over, Graham stayed in touch with the band's bassist Matthew, as they had "lots in common".

The New York rock band formed in 1995, with their biggest hit topping the UK charts in 2000. Their second single, a cover of Erasure's A Little Respect, reached number three.

Frontman Brendan B Brown said agreeing to sponsor the side required little thought.

"We have fans who are no longer fans, they're more like family members, and Graham is one of those guys," he said.

"Graham and Bertie are part of that family."

Brown said the band wanted to help remove financial barriers that could prevent young people from taking part in sport.

"Just knowing that a little bit of funding is out there making it possible for a bunch of kids to get on the pitch, that's really enough for me," he said.

"We weren't always in a position to donate funds to anything - lately that's changed."

Brown added that he thought the new kits looked "rad and totally awesome", and even teased a private gig could be in store as a treat.

"If they really do very well, they do deserve at least an acoustic performance in the locker room," he said.

"Wouldn't that be appropriate, that they get a private show?"

Bertie said it would be "really cool" if Wheatus were ever able to perform for the team.

Brown suggested that could be a possibility, joking that if the players continued their success they might earn such a gig.

articles.title: Alberta rejects secession referendum, chooses to remain part of Canada
articles.summary: The oil-rich province of Alberta has rejected the pathway to secession and will remain part of Canada, landing a definitive blow to a fringe but loud campaign which sought support from the US.
articles.body: The oil-rich province of Alberta has rejected the pathway to secession and will remain part of Canada, landing a definitive blow to a fringe but loud campaign which sought support from the US. About three quarters of voters chose to stay in Canada, while one quarter opted to hold a second vote on separation later as of early Tuesday local time, with roughly 45% of polls reporting, according to unofficial results posted by the province. Monday’s result comes amid a rising tide of patriotism and unity in Canada as the country has rallied against US President Donald Trump’s tariffs and annexation threats. The Alberta independence campaign, a grassroots effort led by a handful of vocal separatists, was amplified heavily online, and some of its leaders had met with members of Trump’s administration. The vote had faced concerns of possible foreign interference after Canadian newspaper the Globe and Mail reported Republican operatives had assisted top separatist leaders with their independence bid. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the vote to remain means that “Albertans and all Canadians will move forward together with renewed purpose and high ambition” in a statement posted to X early Tuesday. Thomas Lukaszuk, former Alberta politician and founder of the pro-unity Forever Canadian movement, said the result would send a strong message to Trump: “Canada is not up for grabs.” “We are a solid country that’s united from coast to coast to coast and we stick up for each other,” Lukaszuk told a cheering crowd as the results came in. Monday’s vote was the first plebiscite of its kind in Canada since the 1995 Quebec referendum, where the predominantly French-speaking province voted against secession by a razor thin margin. Separatism flares amid US tensions Alberta, a province roughly the size of Texas, has long harbored a fringe independence movement. Separatists there argue that Canada’s federal system underrepresents its population of 5 million in parliament, that Canadian efforts to fight climate change threaten Alberta’s lucrative fossil fuel industry and that Alberta’s conservative politics are often outweighed by the more liberal eastern provinces. Though separation frequently polled low in Alberta, the movement grew louder after Carney’s Liberal Party won the 2025 federal elections amid a trade war with the United States. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced in May the province would hold a referendum on whether to remain in Canada, or to have a “binding provincial referendum” on independence later. Over the past two years, secessionist leaders have met with US officials in Washington to try and negotiate support from the Trump administration. Jeffrey Rath, a prominent separatist and lawyer who was part of the group in DC, told CNN last year that Trump’s election in 2024 gave independence activists hope. “If anybody is going to have the guts to recognize an independent Alberta, (it) would be the Trump administration,” Rath said. News of the meetings at the time incensed Canadian politicians, who accused separatist leaders of “treason.” The movement also possesses a Trumpian flavor. Participants at a secessionist rally CNN attended in 2025 donned red MAGA-style “Make Alberta Great Again” hats. A minority even said that Alberta ought to skip independence and become the 51st US state. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has lent support to the separatist cause, saying Albertans are “very independent people” and that the province is a “natural partner for the US” in an interview earlier this year. Last week, Elon Musk, a Trump ally, urged Alberta, along with other Canadian provinces Saskatchewan and Quebec to separate from Canada in a post to his platform X, saying they would be “better off.” Smith said she was “very pleased” with the result to remain in Canada in a post to X late Monday local time, but she has previously cautioned against “demonizing” independence supporters. “We have had, from time to time, these kinds of initiatives flare up,” Smith told CNN in 2025. “And they’re almost always in response to a federal government that’s out of control. But they have all subsided when the federal government got back in its own lane.” Carney, who grew up in Alberta, nodded to that frustration in a speech in Calgary last week urging voters to reject secession. “The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” Carney said. But, the prime minister said, separation would only “burden” Albertans “with years of deep division and great uncertainty.” He also made an oblique swipe at the US. “This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” he said. “The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.” This story has been updated with additional developments.

articles.title: Two Canadian entrepreneurs built a sleep-products brand in four years; Hush hit a C$48 million valuation before Sleep Country bought 52%
articles.summary: Two Canadian entrepreneurs turned a weighted blanket business into a sleep-products brand that attracted a major buyer within four years.
articles.body: Two Canadian entrepreneurs turned a weighted blanket business into a sleep-products brand that attracted a major buyer within four years. Aaron Spivak and Lior Ohayon founded Hush after exploring how weighted blankets could help people sleep better. Their first product gained traction, but customers soon complained that it was too hot for summer. The founders used this feedback to develop a cooling version, which attracted thousands of backers on Kickstarter. Their growing business caught the attention of Canadian retailer Sleep Country Canada, which bought a 52% stake in Hush for C$25 million in October 2021. The deal valued the company at C$48 million.How two Canadian entrepreneurs built Hush in four yearsHush was founded in 2017 by Aaron Spivak and Lior Ohayon. The company launched its weighted blanket in Canada in 2018. In a December 2025 interview with Forbes, Spivak explained how the idea took shape. Ohayon had volunteered at a summer camp for children with special needs, where he encountered a sensory room with a weighted device. That experience helped inspire the pair to explore weighted blankets and deep-touch pressure stimulation. The founders spent about six months developing their first blanket while holding down full-time jobs. Spivak said they worked on Hush between 5 pm and 1 am and initially tested demand through pre-orders.The early response was encouraging. Spivak told Forbes that monthly sales rose from C$30,000 in the first month to C$60,000, C$120,000 and C$300,000 over the following months. These are figures reported by the founder, not independently audited results.Customer feedback led to a cooling blanketThe early momentum did not last uninterrupted. During Hush's first summer, sales slowed as customers complained that the weighted blanket became too hot in warmer weather. Spivak told Forbes that the founders surveyed 500 customers to understand the problem. The feedback pointed to a clear opportunity: retain the appeal of a weighted blanket while making it cooler to use.The founders responded with Hush Iced, a cooling weighted blanket. They launched it on Kickstarter in March 2019, setting a funding target of C$25,000. The campaign ran from March 13 to April 12 and raised C$1,116,334 from 5,394 backers. That was more than 44 times the original funding target. The response helped Hush expand beyond its first product. The company went on to sell pillows, sheets, mattresses and other sleep accessories, turning a single-product idea into a broader sleep-products business.Hush grew into a wider sleep-products brandHush's expanding product range attracted the attention of Sleep Country Canada, a major Canadian mattress and sleep-products retailer. By October 2021, Hush offered weighted blankets, pillows, sheets and mattresses. Sleep Country described the company as an eight-figure brand within its first 24 months.Spivak also told Forbes that Hush grew from approximately C$700,000 in its first year to a C$10 million business. The expansion gave Hush a broader presence in the sleep-products market. It also offered Sleep Country an opportunity to strengthen its digital business and add an established direct-to-consumer brand to its portfolio.Sleep Country bought 52% of Hush in 2021In October 2021, Canadian retailer Sleep Country acquired a 52% stake in Hush for C$25 million, valuing the sleep-products brand at C$48 million. The deal came just four years after Hush was founded, with co-founders Aaron Spivak and Lior Ohayon remaining involved in the business.Sleep Country gradually increased its ownership, acquiring another 16% stake in 2023. In May 2024, it bought the remaining shares, bringing Hush fully under its ownership.Hush continued to expand its product rangeHush continued developing its product portfolio after becoming part of Sleep Country. In April 2025, the company introduced Hush Little Baby, a product line for babies and toddlers. articles.title: Alberta rejects move toward independence from Canada in a victory for Carney
articles.summary: Voters in Canada’s oil-rich province of Alberta have rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. projected early Tuesday.
articles.body: EDMONTON, Alberta — Voters in Canada’s oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with early referendum results Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for national unity amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats. With more than 1.5 million votes counted, 76% supported remaining in Canada, while close to 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta. The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada. “Albertans made a clear choice,” Carney said. “They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.” Carney said that the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its center. Alberta’s separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media. Smith, who called the referendum amid pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party, or UCP, despite opposing independence, said that she would address the province Tuesday evening about the results and Alberta’s future. “We are a solid country that’s united from coast to coast to coast,” Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters. Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday. Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada’s federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. Despite the proposal’s apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that won’t disappear. Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. “Vote like Canada’s future depends on it, because it does,” he told a rally on Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up. Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over Covid-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said. Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. At a separatist referendum night gathering at an Edmonton restaurant, the crowd fell quiet as results rolled in. “We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project. “We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.” Rath had said he would be thrilled if 30% of Albertans voted to begin the separation process. He wants Smith ousted as leader of her governing United Conservative Party and said the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party. Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said that Albertans have long been mistreated by Canada’s federal government. “Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony,” he said after voting Monday. “They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything.” Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a “referendum on a referendum” rather than healthcare. With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we’re fighting among ourselves.”

articles.title: Southeast Asia’s haze crisis will persist until polluters pay
articles.summary: Cheap land clearing imposes costs across borders. ASEAN must change the incentives that keep the fires burning.
articles.body:
Across Southeast Asia, the haze has returned with a familiar cruelty. Malaysia has closed schools as air quality deteriorated, Singapore has experienced dangerous levels of air pollution, and even parts of the Philippines have been affected, underscoring how far the smoke has travelled. In Indonesia, meanwhile, forest and peatland fires, a major source of the region’s haze, have threatened communities and livelihoods, particularly in parts of Kalimantan. What begins as land burning in one country can become a public health emergency across an entire region.

The immediate response is predictable: extinguish fires, distribute masks and seek regional cooperation. All are necessary, but none explains why the emergency keeps returning. Malaysian children missing school, Singaporean residents breathing polluted air, Filipino communities exposed to drifting smoke and Indonesian families living near burning land all bear different costs from the same regional failure.

Dry weather and El Nino can intensify fires, but many are deliberately started to clear land for agriculture. The deeper question is why practices that create enormous public losses can remain attractive to those who benefit from them. When the gains from cheap land preparation are concentrated while the costs of smoke are dispersed across communities and national borders, the market signal is distorted and political responsibility becomes easier to evade.

The haze is therefore not merely an environmental emergency or a test of diplomatic goodwill. It disrupts ordinary life, strains public services and exposes how easily environmental costs can be shifted away from those who create them. It is a failure of economic accountability. Unless Southeast Asia changes who pays for the damage, how land-clearing decisions are monitored and what consequences follow proven violations, each dry season will bring another round of emergency measures followed by familiar arguments over blame.

Fire can be an inexpensive way to clear vegetation, especially where land governance is weak, alternative methods are costly and enforcement is uncertain. The private calculation is straightforward: spend less on land preparation and capture the returns. The fires cause respiratory illness, lost working days, school closures and transport disruption, while also damaging ecosystems and releasing greenhouse gases. Those costs are rarely borne in full by those responsible for the burning.

The World Bank’s assessment of Indonesia’s 2015 fire crisis estimated losses of at least $16.1bn, equivalent to 1.9 percent of that year’s gross domestic product (GDP). Government figures put the area burned between June and October at 2.6 million hectares. The bank linked the fires to cheap land preparation, drought and weak enforcement. Its estimate covered agriculture, trade, tourism, transport, healthcare and emergency response, but excluded some long-term health damage and lost ecosystem services.

That figure is not a price tag for the 2026 fires. It shows the scale of losses a recurrent crisis can impose. More recent estimates put the area burned in Indonesia this year at between 637,000 and 900,000 hectares, while Ministry of Health data recorded 283,270 cases of respiratory illness linked to the fires in seven provinces as of October 13. In West Kalimantan province, fires have also threatened communities and livelihoods, underscoring that Indonesians living beside the flames bear costs long before smoke reaches neighbouring countries.

This is the central economic distortion: the cost of burning is not fully reflected in the decision to burn. When benefits accrue privately, but health costs, lost income and ecological damage are borne by society, fire can remain economically attractive even when its total cost is enormous. Small farmers need affordable, practical alternatives to burning; companies must face credible liability when evidence links them to fires; and peatlands need sustained restoration and water management, not emergency attention only when smoke becomes politically embarrassing.

Smoke travels across borders, but responsibility and enforcement remain largely national. Tracing pollution to a particular fire, identifying those responsible and proving cross-border harm can be difficult. A satellite hotspot is a warning signal, but not by itself proof of who started a fire or whether a company is liable.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is not without rules. Its Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution was signed in 2002 and entered into force in 2003; Indonesia ratified it in 2014. The region also has a Haze-Free Roadmap and a strategy for sustainable peatland management for 2023-30. But agreements cannot substitute consistent implementation, transparent enforcement or incentives that make prevention economically rational.

The challenge is translating these commitments into effective action. Cooperation can improve monitoring and preparedness, but ASEAN’s consensus-based diplomacy has limited leverage when national enforcement is inconsistent or commercial interests resist scrutiny. Its investment framework for haze-free land management aims to mobilise $1.5bn by 2030. Yet money alone will not suffice without transparent spending, measurable outcomes and accountability for repeated fires.

This does not mean every fire is caused by a large corporation or that all pollution in Kuala Lumpur or Singapore originates in Indonesia. Local emissions and weather conditions matter, and fires may involve companies, smallholders or other actors. Accountability requires investigations that identify those responsible and distinguish proven violations from suspicion. Blanket blame lets offenders disappear into arguments about sovereignty, while a lack of transparent evidence erodes trust between neighbours.

ASEAN foreign ministers are due to discuss the haze crisis at preparatory meetings before the bloc’s November summit in Manila. Their discussions should be judged by whether they shift the region from managing haze to preventing it.

First, member states should publish comparable data on burned areas, fire recurrence, concessions and enforcement outcomes. Satellite detections should be cross-checked with field investigations, and concession maps should be made available for scrutiny by communities and independent researchers. Greater transparency would make it harder to obscure responsibility through competing claims.

Second, governments should put the polluter-pays principle into practice. Where investigations establish responsibility, penalties and restoration orders should reflect the damage caused, while repeat violations should trigger stronger consequences. Environmental liability must be evidence-based and applied consistently, not used as a political weapon. Penalties must also be substantial enough to deter violations rather than simply become a cost of doing business.

Third, prevention must be economically viable. Smallholders need machinery, technical assistance, credit and access to markets to make alternatives to burning affordable. Peatland rewetting, firebreaks and community-based monitoring require predictable funding before the dry season, rather than ad hoc budgets after fires spread. ASEAN’s investment framework can help mobilise resources, but governments should disclose where funds go and assess their impact on reductions in fires and smoke exposure.

Finally, ASEAN should publish a regional scorecard tied to its 2030 haze-free goal. It should track not only hotspots and hectares burned, but also repeat fires, response times, enforcement, peatland restoration, school closures and population exposure to dangerous air. No regional mechanism can replace Indonesia’s responsibility to prevent fires on its territory. But sovereignty cannot mean that the costs of domestic land-use decisions are ignored once smoke crosses a border. The principle should be simple: those who profit from risky practices must not be allowed to transfer the bill to children missing school, workers losing wages, sick families or neighbouring states.

For more than two decades, ASEAN has had agreements, strategies and roadmaps. The haze’s return does not make these efforts worthless; it shows prevention remains inadequate. If leaders leave November’s meetings with another declaration but no transparent metrics, credible enforcement and funding for alternatives, the region will once again treat the symptoms while preserving the incentives that produce them. Economic accountability is not an add-on to haze policy. It is the condition for making that policy work.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Palestine weekly: Israeli settlers attack journalist and diplomats
articles.summary: Settler olive harvest attacks top 2025 total, journalist and diplomats attacked as Israel halts Gaza commercial imports.
articles.body:
With more than a month left of the olive harvest season to go, United Nations deputy spokesperson Farhan Haq said on Friday that the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) had recorded more than 200 Israeli attacks on Palestinian farmers since September 1, eclipsing the 185 that OCHA documented across the entire 2025 harvest season.

The attacks have already killed one Palestinian, injured more than 120 and damaged more than 2,500 trees. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 34 Israeli attacks on Friday that injured at least 19 people , with another 40 on Saturday.

Israeli settlers are carrying out such widescale attacks and thefts with backing from some religious figures. On Friday, Rabbi Dov Lior, spiritual guide of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party, ruled that settlers may take olives from Palestinian orchards, proclaiming “Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish settlements in order to publicly demonstrate our ownership of the land and thereby fulfill the commandment of conquering the land”.

“An olive tree today is more significant in the campaign for Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank] than an M16 rifle,” said one post in a settler chat group this week.

“Settlers are stealing the Palestinian olive crop on a vast scale, never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue,” said Sarit Michaeli, formerly the international advocacy director of the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem.

Under this ideological push, dozens of attacks on olive harvesters have been reported each day. On October 16, in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, about 80 masked settlers armed with clubs charged at Palestinians picking olives . During the attack, Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, 63, fell and was beaten for more than 10 minutes by settlers, videos and her own account attest. She suffered broken ribs and needed hand surgery, while her camera, phone and passport were stolen. Israeli activist Jonathan Pollak reported that soldiers later shot a village council member, Abdel Jaber Obeid, in the thigh.

Then, on Saturday, masked settlers with clubs attacked a delegation visiting Taybeh, east of Ramallah, that included Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats, and church representatives. A window of a Belgian consulate vehicle was smashed. French mayor Bernard Baudoux, 78, was kicked and beaten during the attack.

In response to these incidents, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was “very disturbed”, while US Ambassador Mike Huckabee called Levine’s attack “a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”. France demanded arrests and the European Union said it expected “full accountability”.

In response, Israel’s military called the Taybeh attack “severe”, and leader of the Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, described settler violence as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the government of Israel”, according to The Times of Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office, however, offered a conditional condemnation of Levine’s attack, saying questions remained about “who initiated the violence”. After the attack in Taybeh, his office equivocated on the matter, too, remarking that “the more serious the accusation, the stronger the evidence required”.

On Monday, police and the domestic intelligence agency Shin Bet launched “Operation Olive Leaf”, arresting 10 Israelis in raids near Ofra and Shiloh in connection to these attacks on foreign journalists and diplomats.

However, no other arrests or investigations have been announced for the dozens of other settler attacks against Palestinians reported this weekend alone. Beyond the headline incidents, masked settlers – often alongside soldiers – targeted farmers, flocks, homes and land.

Settlers beat two women in Beit Lid on Tuesday and injured an American citizen, Haytham Tayseer, in Burqa on Thursday, leaving him with deep head wounds.

Six people, including four women and a child, were injured in Ma’in, in Masafer Yatta, on Saturday, the Red Crescent said.

Settlers burned four vehicles in Turmus Aya, including a civil defence vehicle, and set fire to a mosque in Mikhmas , the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

Settlers stabbed to death about 20 sheep in Kafr Malek, Mayor Najeh Rustum told Al Jazeera.

Bulldozers uprooted hundreds of olive trees in Kafr Malek, and settlers cut down 120 olive trees in Kisan, near Bethlehem, Wafa reported.

In Gaza, the ever-worsening humanitarian situation is now deteriorating even more rapidly. Israel declared on October 14 that no commercial goods would be allowed to enter Gaza, blaming a dispute between merchants and Hamas over a 10,000-shekel ($3,220) per-truck fee. Gaza’s Government Media Office called that a “ blatant disinformation campaign ”, saying the sum was a voluntary contribution to a fund for widows and orphans. By Sunday, prices had jumped significantly: a carton of eggs rose in price from 35 shekels ($11.30) to 60-70 shekels ($18-$21), and a sack of flour from 25-35 shekels ($7.50-$10.50) to about 80 shekels ($24), residents said.

Such price increases are taking place just as the World Food Programme announced this week it would cut the number of people it feeds monthly in Gaza from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. Gaza’s Health Ministry said 466 people have died of malnutrition since 2024 and 67 percent of the population faces crisis-level food insecurity or worse through year-end.

Meanwhile, Israeli forces continued to kill Palestinians in Gaza each day. As of October 19, Gaza’s Health Ministry put the toll since last year’s “ceasefire” at 1,522 killed and 5,421 wounded – 27 killed in the past week, against 33 the previous week and 38 the week before. The cumulative death toll has reached 74,480 since October 7, 2023.

Three children, including Muhammad Riyad Abu Hammad, 14, in Deir el-Balah – the Education Ministry said shrapnel pierced his school bag on his way home from school on Saturday – and Misk Hazem al-Dalu and Tamer Shadi Subh, who were killed in the Maghazi camp and Beit Lahiya, respectively, on Sunday. UNICEF said more than 340 children have been killed since the ceasefire .

Drone strikes in the past week killed Ahmad Raja al-Shaer and Basel Nabil Qeshta in al-Qarara; Reem Awad in a strike on a Gaza City apartment; Mahmoud al-Madhoun and Ubaida Murtaja in Gaza City; Abdullah and Imad Jaber and Sheikh Majid al-Sabbagh, a Quran school director in Tuffah, on October 17; Amer al-Horani near a Jabalia clinic the same day; and police officer Abd al-Jawad Joudeh in Rafah.

Shootings killed Saddam al-Za’anin in Jabalia, Hatem Abu Hasanein by quadcopter fire, Huda Abu Adwan, 49, in al-Mawasi and Wijdan Shurrab, 28, in eastern Khan Younis, according to Wafa and local activists.

Israel’s military said several of those killed this week were Hamas members. None of its claims has been independently verified.

Meanwhile, Israeli forces continued advancing the “Yellow Line” deeper into Shujayea on Saturday, placing concrete blocks on al-Qa’qa Street. The line demarcates areas under Israeli control, which now extend across about 65 percent of Gaza, far beyond what was envisaged under last year’s “ceasefire” agreement.

articles.title: US-Ukraine relations sour as Trump, Zelenskyy clash over talks, arms
articles.summary: Trump calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as negotiator, while Ukraine’s president says arms shipments delayed.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump says someone other than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should negotiate on Kyiv’s behalf in talks to end Russia’s war.

“Zelenskyy is a man that should have had settled this war a long time ago. If he would’ve listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Monday. “Maybe it’s time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate.”

The US president has been verbally swiping at his Ukrainian counterpart for several days as a rift between the leaders deepens.

On Sunday, Trump claimed on Truth Social that Zelenskyy does not want to end the war. Earlier this month, he called for him to be replaced as president , and labelled him a “warmonger” over Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries .

Trump has also defended sanctions waivers for Russia, saying in the same Truth Social post that he wants to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

Zelenskyy said the decision “will hurt Ukraine” and strengthen Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war effort.

Trump also announced plans on October 9 for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets to tackle fuel prices that have soared since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February.

The decision has angered not only Kyiv, but also European partners and US officials, who say it rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war on Ukraine.

Zelenskyy told US senators at a meeting on Monday that decisions taken by the Trump administration “are hard to explain between friends”.

He said arms shipments had been delayed and intelligence sharing restricted.

“We also know that … the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for through the PURL (Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List) programme,” he said.

To his knowledge, he added, one missile package was waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

He also said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were awaiting US approval.

In remarks posted in a video on Telegram, Zelenskyy said that on three occasions in the past week, Ukraine had not received the advance warning of Russian attacks generally provided by its partners.

Last week, Zelenskyy suggested a disruption of Starlink services in Ukraine was “deliberate”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected the claim.

The sparring comes as Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff is ⁠set to travel to Norway this week for the next round of negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine, the Reuters news agency reported, citing three people familiar with the matter.

Two of the sources said they expected Zelenskyy to attend the meetings.

The Oslo discussions are expected to include Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, representatives of the E4 – made up of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Poland – the European Union, and NATO.

articles.title: Suspect arrested after Limoges town hall set alight during disorder - French media
articles.summary: The spire of the clock tower at Limoges city hall dramatically collapsed as it was engulfed in flames on Saturday.
articles.body:
A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.

The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.

The 40-year-old suspect is known for acts of violence against public officials and has been classified as an "S" subject, meaning he is a potential threat to national security, FranceInfo reported.

More than 120 people have already been imprisoned following widespread demonstrations across France, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told CNews-Europe.

Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.

Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".

The justice minister insisted France did not need to be put into a state of emergency which would "deprive all French people of their individual freedoms".

But French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu earlier said he had not ruled out imposing a state of emergency.

Targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder, Lecornu said.

Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.

Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.

Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.

Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.

Earlier Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez admitted police had "lost control" in some cities.

He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.

More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.

Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.

More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.

Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.

Protest organisers have declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France.

The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.
