articles.title: A space-industry entrepreneur made his first million at 27 but plans to leave his children only an eight-figure inheritance; will donate the bulk of his wealth to philanthropy
articles.summary: Dylan Taylor, chairman and CEO of space technology company Voyager Technologies, made his first million at 27.
articles.body: Dylan Taylor, chairman and CEO of space technology company Voyager Technologies, made his first million at 27. Now a billionaire, he plans to leave his two children an eight-figure inheritance rather than pass down his entire fortune. In a May 27, 2026, interview with Fortune, Taylor said he would direct the wealth beyond that limit towards philanthropy. His fortune grew through business leadership, real estate and investments, and increased further after Voyager went public in 2025. Taylor believes passing down enormous fortunes may not benefit children or society. Instead, he wants his wealth to address unmet needs and support causes that can make a difference during his lifetime.How a space entrepreneur made his first million at 27Taylor built his career across real estate, finance and technology before moving into the commercial space industry. He held senior leadership roles at Colliers International, including global president and chief operating officer, and served in executive and board positions at other companies.His approach to building wealth involved more than earning a salary. Taylor invested in real estate and emerging businesses, including companies in the space sector. He has said that these investments, alongside his executive career, helped him build his fortune.Taylor later became chairman and CEO of Voyager Technologies, a company focused on space technology, infrastructure and national security. His career eventually brought together his business experience and interest in commercial space exploration.Voyager's stock market debut boosted his fortuneVoyager Technologies went public on the New York Stock Exchange in June 2025. The company priced its initial public offering at US$31 per share. On its first day of trading, the shares opened at US$69.75, giving Voyager a market valuation of approximately US$3.8 billion at the time.The listing marked a major milestone for Taylor. Fortune reported in May 2026 that his net worth had crossed the billion-dollar mark in 2025, helped by Voyager's IPO, his real estate portfolio and investments in companies including Robinhood, Relativity Space and Calm.Voyager's valuation does not represent Taylor's personal wealth. His fortune also depends on his ownership stake and other assets and investments.Why he wants to limit his children's inheritanceTaylor has two children and believes they should receive enough money to be financially secure without inheriting a fortune so large that they have little incentive to build something themselves.In his interview with Fortune, he said he was not a strong believer in transferring wealth across generations. When asked how much his children could expect to inherit, he described the amount as “eight figures, not nine”. That means tens of millions of dollars rather than hundreds of millions.Taylor said his children are old enough to access the resources available to them but have not used them because they want to achieve things independently. He sees this as a positive outcome and wants to preserve that sense of independence.His plan is to provide a substantial financial safety net while directing the rest of his wealth towards causes beyond his family.He wants the bulk of his wealth to support philanthropyTaylor plans to direct the wealth beyond his children's inheritance towards philanthropic causes. According to Fortune, the amount could eventually reach hundreds of millions of dollars or more.One of the causes closest to him is Space for Humanity, a nonprofit he founded in 2017. The organisation aims to expand access to spaceflight and use the experience of seeing Earth from space to encourage people to address global challenges.Taylor has also supported initiatives that help widen access to careers in the space industry, including the Brooke Owens Fellowship, the Patti Grace Smith Fellowship and Mission: Astro Access.His approach centres on using wealth to address needs that remain unmet. Rather than preserving the bulk of his fortune in trusts for descendants far into the future, he wants it to support causes that can make a difference during his lifetime.His approach echoes Bill Gates' inheritance plansTaylor's position resembles that of Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, who has said he plans to leave his children less than 1% of his wealth and direct most of his fortune towards philanthropy.Other wealthy individuals have also questioned whether passing down enormous fortunes is the best use of their money. Laurene Powell Jobs, who inherited wealth from Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, has said she does not intend to pass her fortune down through generations. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has also discussed directing much of his wealth towards charitable causes.These approaches reflect a wider debate over inheritance, financial independence and the concentration of wealth. Supporters of large inheritances argue that they provide security and opportunities for future generations. Critics contend that enormous fortunes can concentrate resources within a small number of families and reduce incentives for independent achievement.Taylor's position is that his children should have financial security while the bulk of his fortune serves a wider purpose.A different view of generational wealthTaylor's inheritance plan marks a contrast between how he accumulated his fortune and how he wants it used. He built wealth through executive roles, investments and the growth of Voyager Technologies, but does not intend to pass all of it to his children.His stated plan is to leave them an eight-figure inheritance and direct the remainder towards philanthropy. articles.title: Alberta voters reject separation from Canada, early results show
articles.summary: With more than one million votes counted, about 77 percent supported remaining in Canada.
articles.body:
Alberta residents have voted to remain ⁠part of Canada in the province’s first-ever referendum on separation, in a much-needed win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he ‌attempts to unify the country amid an ongoing trade war with the United States.

With more than one million votes counted, about 77 percent supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23 percent who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation, early results showed on Tuesday.

The vote was not a direct referendum on independence but would have set oil-rich Alberta on a path towards a future vote on separation from Canada.

Carney welcomed the result and said Albertans had made a “clear choice” in favour of unity.

“They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other,” he said in a statement on X.

Jeffrey Rath, a top leader of the secessionist Alberta Prosperity Project, told reporters his push for an independent Alberta will “absolutely” continue, despite the result from Monday’s vote.

“We’ve learned a lot of lessons from this fight,” he said.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, a conservative, said she voted against independence but called the referendum to settle an issue that has divided the province.

She has said a win for the federalists would close the secession question.

Alberta has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, and much of the secessionist momentum has been driven by anger over oil industry management.

Smith has blamed Carney’s predecessor Justin Trudeau for igniting the secessionist fire, accusing him of trying to crush oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda.

Alberta’s independence push has also drawn sustained interest from the allies of US President Donald Trump, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who called Alberta Washington’s “natural partner”. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and eminent Trump supporter, also posted on X that Alberta “should separate”.

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has worked to improve relations between the province and Ottawa since taking office last year. He has partnered with Smith on advancing a new pipeline to export more Alberta bitumen overseas, a project considered a nonstarter during Trudeau’s tenure.

articles.title: Morocco’s not-so-new government faces new challenges
articles.summary: The new cabinet has doubled down on continuity at a time of regional turmoil and domestic anxiety.
articles.body:
On October 16, King Mohammed VI of Morocco appointed a new government headed by Prime Minister Fatima Zohra Al Mansouri. This is the first time in Moroccan history that a woman is leading the government – a precedent that was covered widely in international media.

In the Moroccan context, however, what is important is that Al Mansouri hails from the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), which won the most seats in parliamentary elections in September. The party was founded by Ali Himma, a close associate and adviser to the king.

PAM, which has formed a coalition with three other parties, dominates the new government. This signals continuity rather than potential for change.

When thinking about what trajectory the new government is likely to take, it is important to consider PAM’s evolution.

The party was established in 2008 with the aim of countering the rise of political Islam in Morocco and in particular, the Justice and Development Party (PJD). The Arab Spring, which saw mass protests across the country, brought changes to the Moroccan political scene, allowing more space for political forces like the PJD and, to an extent, curbing the influence of the establishment, known as the Makhzen.

In 2011, Himma distanced himself from PAM and became an adviser to the king. Yet, the party continued to be perceived by other political groups as tied to the Makhzen.

For years, PAM carried the stigma of its origins, but it persisted in trying to gain acceptance. In the 2016 elections, it challenged the PJD and secured the second-biggest number of votes, thus establishing itself as a legitimate political force. Yet this was still not enough to enable it to lead the government.

The party subsequently reinvented itself by rejuvenating its ranks and gaining experience in public affairs through its participation in the 2021 government as a coalition partner. In the latest elections, PAM finally won.

This election victory, however, needs to be put into perspective: 62 percent of eligible voters stayed away from the polls. On election day, the authorities had to call on people to go out and vote.

Apart from the low turnout, there were suspicions of irregularities, but because in some cases the official election records were not released, observers and political parties were unable to obtain tangible evidence.

There was also the familiar phenomenon of influential figures being brought into political parties at the last minute to boost electoral prospects. For example, just two months before the election, Faouzi Laaqjea, president of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation, whose popularity stems from the achievements of Moroccan football, officially joined PAM.

To secure a majority in parliament, the party has had to form a coalition with forces which had previously questioned its legitimacy. While PAM has gained legitimacy through this alliance, the other parties and their leaders may now lose credibility.

The newly formed government has retained more than half the members of its predecessor, not to mention the so-called sovereign ministries, which fall directly within the king’s reserved powers. Some Moroccans are already asking what was the point of holding elections if the same people are brought back to govern.

The new government has an ambitious programme to respond to growing domestic pressure as the cost-of-living crisis deepens. At the first Council of Ministers meeting chaired by the king on October 17 , a 2027 Finance Bill was put forward that featured greater emphasis on addressing social issues, citizens’ purchasing power and youth inclusion.

However, this agenda is facing an unfavourable international economic and financial environment, marked by rising energy prices and increasing costs of inputs for some of Morocco’s leading sectors, including phosphate production.

The state-owned OCP Group, which is in charge of phosphate extraction and the industrial processing of phosphate derivatives and is one of Morocco’s principal sources of wealth, is now experiencing difficult times.

There are also concerns about the potential effects of El Nino, which could bring more dry weather and threaten food security in a country that just endured seven consecutive years of drought.

Tourism, another major source of revenue, could also suffer from the global slowdown in travel, rising transport costs and the uncertainties arising from tensions in the Gulf and Europe.

The circumstances are therefore far from favourable for the new government, and public opinion appears broadly sceptical.

Last but not least, this government will face an experienced and outspoken opposition, represented by both the Islamist PJD and the radical left.

Even the ministers holding the so-called sovereign portfolios face serious challenges. The foreign minister must contend with public opposition to the normalisation of relations with Israel. The interior minister has to tackle allegations of electoral manipulation.

The minister of religious affairs is facing the fallout of controversial statements concerning Morocco as a secular country and remarks about Ceuta, known in Morocco as Sebta, made during a religious ceremony. These comments were poorly received by the Spanish authorities.

The new government has an ambitious agenda, indeed, but its tenure will be shaped by difficult circumstances – both at home and abroad – that are largely out of its control.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Iconic 1880s Rhode Island waterfront social club is being offered for the first time in 50 years; after a $1.2 million price cut, the historic five-bedroom property now asks $9.75 million
articles.summary: The Reading Room, one of Narragansett's most iconic properties, has hit the market for the first time in over 50 years.
articles.body: The Reading Room, one of Narragansett's most iconic properties, has hit the market for the first time in over 50 years. The five-bedroom house is for sale for $9.75 million after a price cut. It was first listed in June at $10.95 million, Realtor.com reported. Built in 1880 as a social club, the property stands beside The Towers and is the last surviving remnant of the grand Narragansett Pier Casino.Back in the day, it was a men's club with a bed and breakfastThe house began in the late 1800s as a liquor-free men's club. “It was originally a social club in the 1880s and was a reading room where men would gather to smoke cigars,” listing agent John Hodnett of Hopewell Real Estate told the outlet. Historian Winifred J.W. Kissouth described it as a liquor-free men's bed-and-breakfast club where members went to read and smoke, according to The Boston Globe. Some of its famous visitors included Jerome Bonaparte, a relative of Napoleon Bonaparte, and New York surgeon Dr Charles Hitchcock.A historic club with a waterfront viewThe building did not stay where it was originally built. The Reading Room was moved from Mathewson Street to its present location on Ocean Road in the late 1890s, according to documentation from the National Register of Historic Places. The move made it part of the Narragansett Pier Casino. At the time, ‘casino’ often referred to social clubs rather than gambling halls, which surprises many visitors today.“It was relocated to its current location to be a part of the casino. Now, it’s ideally located minutes away from the town beach, cafes and restaurants,” Hodnett added.The neighbouring building is The Towers, the only surviving remnant of the casino after a series of fires, nor'easters and hurricanes. From the house, you can see both the bay and the landmark, and the view is a big reason people remember the property.In 2010, the house underwent a major restoration that brought back its Victorian character. The project received historic-preservation recognition from Preserve Rhode Island and the Rhody Awards. Many of its original features survived, including the hardwood floors, bay windows, grand staircase, stained glass, high ceilings, period chandeliers and three fireplaces.“This property enjoys sweeping water-view porches, water views from almost every room, intricate details, multiple year-round sun porches, historic chandeliers and a unique Tower Room,” the listing on Sotheby's Realty says. It describes the home as a “once-in-a-generation opportunity” to live in the heart of Narragansett.The house sits on 0.69 acres and spans 5,099 square feet, with five bedrooms, two full bathrooms and two half-bathrooms. Most historic homes on Narragansett Pier sit on smaller parcels, so this one offers something rare. Hodnett describes the setting as a village address with the feel of a private sanctuary. The property also includes a detached three-car garage, a covered front porch and multiple sunrooms, so the outdoor space is not limited to the lawn.The home could serve as the buyer's primary residence. According to the agent, much of the hard work has already been done. The restoration is complete, and a new owner can focus on shaping the interior to suit their lifestyle rather than repairing the structure.In June, the property was listed for $10.95 million. After sitting on the market for months, the price has fallen to $9.75 million. It is unclear why the price was reduced.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Revolut down as thousands of users report app not working
articles.summary: Some users of the British neobank reported being unable to make some payments or access funds in its app on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Revolut has been hit by an outage which it says is impacting "multiple services", as thousands of customers report problems.

Users of the British bank have flagged being unable to make some payments or access funds via its app on Tuesday morning.

Platform outage monitor Downdetector had seen more than 1,500 user reports of issues with Revolut services shortly after 08:00 BST.

"We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services," a Revolut spokesperson told the BBC - adding "we can confirm that all our customers' money and data are safe."

"We've been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused," they added.

A page on the company's website showed a range of services were "partially unavailable" - including card payments, transfers, ATM withdrawals and its customer support services to be having issues.

On social media, a number of users have criticised the company over the outage - saying it left them unable to access funds, make payments or contact customer support.

Revolut is one of a handful of so-called "neobanks" that sprung up to rival traditional banks with a digital-first approach to financial services.

According to its website, the bank has more than 80 million customers worldwide.

The company has not clarified whether the issues it was experiencing on Tuesday were affecting users globally.

Revolut also declined to say what was causing its service issues.

But other popular services, including Lloyds Bank and Bank of Scotland - both owned by Lloyds Banking Group - were also reportedly experiencing some problems on Tuesday.

A Lloyds spokesperson told the BBC its app was functioning normally, but said "we understand some are having issues with certain online services this morning".

"We are aware of similar issues affecting other organisations and are monitoring the situation closely," they added.

Some have linked the issues seemingly affecting multiple sites in the UK to an incident reported by Google Cloud on Tuesday .

According to a Google Cloud service health dashboard, it has been experiencing "elevated errors and intermittent network failures" at across some of its services at its UK cloud facility, europe-west2.

articles.title: French protests: Is it game over for Macron’s centrists before elections?
articles.summary: The protests have further polarised the French and turned the youth into a key, angry, voting bloc.
articles.body:
Paris, France – After nationwide protests turned violent, French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday night tried to strike a balance between acknowledging the concerns of students demanding changes to the education system and criticising rioters.

“Those who have destroyed property must pay. Those who have looted must reimburse their victims. Those who sought to bring down the republic will be held accountable,” Macron said.

But the president’s speech was not what Yanis, a 20-year-old from Ivry-sur-Seine, a suburb just southeast of Paris, wanted to hear.

“He gave his usual ‘bla bla bla speech’ without putting forward anything concrete,” he said. “We’ll be back on the streets anyway. There will be one demonstration after another until something changes – every weekend, without a break”.

As France grapples with widespread anger that bubbled over in the form of violent protests last weekend, appetite – at least among the country’s youth – for centrist politics of the kind that Macron represents appears to be rapidly shrinking.

The unrest in France comes months before the country’s 2027 presidential election and has further sharpened political divisions, with parties seeking to present themselves as the answer to the frustration visible on the streets.

The populist-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon has embraced the student movement with enthusiasm, while far-right firebrand Marine Le Pen has focused on the disorder that came with the demonstrations, framing it as a crisis of security and authority. The centrist Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has accused the extreme left of instigating violence as a “warm-up round” for the presidential election.

Polling before the election points to a contest in which both the far left and the far right could play a central role. But while the country is demanding change, there is little consensus on what that change should look like. Macron, who has been in power for two terms, will need to step aside after the election, as the constitution bars him from running again.

“Candidates have no choice but to take a stand and address young people,” said political analyst Beligh Nabli, a professor of public law at UPEC-Paris XII. “They have a political obligation to have a message aimed at young people. That message must not be empty, but it will have to answer their demands.”

Since launching their protest in mid-September, students have demanded better schools, more teachers and a more equal system. But the movement quickly spilled out of the schoolyards and into the streets, tapping into broader social and economic anxieties.

The protests have brought these issues to the centre of the political debate in a way that might not otherwise have happened, given young people’s comparatively low electoral participation and the tendency of political campaigns to focus on older voters and issues such as pensions, say analysts.

“If it wasn’t for this mobilisation, it would have been business as usual,” Nabli said. “We would have seen a kind of relative indifference from the candidates towards young people because they are not the social group that mobilises the most in elections, in contrast with those over 60.”

France Unbowed – La France Insoumise (LFI) in French – the left party led by Melenchon, has strongly supported the student movement to the point that critics have accused the party of spurring youth resentment and exploiting the unrest for political gain. Yet the party’s appeal among young voters predates the protests. Its programme addresses several of the movement’s central grievances, including investment in education, teachers’ pay and the abolition of Parcoursup, an online platform students must use for higher education applications that many say lacks transparency.

According to an OpinionWay poll for Les Echos, published on Thursday, Melenchon leads among voters aged 18 to 24, with 49 percent backing him – a 10-percentage-point increase compared with 2022.

For some young protesters, support for Melenchon reflects both opposition to the far right and frustration with the political centre.

“I’m going to vote for La France Insoumise to counter the far right, the National Rally, and the centre, which is basically going to give us a repeat of Macron’s policies,” said Lydia, 21, a student at the Ecole du Louvre who took part in a protest at the museum on Monday.

But she said she was under no illusion that the party would necessarily solve France’s problems. She also criticised what she sees as the demonisation of LFI by critics, arguing that even moderately left-wing positions are increasingly labelled extreme. “It’s becoming rather exceptional to have empathy; it’s becoming something extreme left-wing,” she said.

On the other side of the political spectrum, Le Pen and her National Rally party have sought to make the unrest a question of law and order, accusing the government of failing to be able to control the country, and its main competitor, Melenchon, of stoking violence. Le Pen remains the leading contender in the presidential race with 32 percent of the vote, while the National Rally ranked second among voters aged 18 to 24, behind France Unbowed.

“Yesterday, you saw our cities, our streets, and our country mistreated, battered, and looted,” Le Pen said in a video message on Sunday night. “We are experiencing a profound crisis of trust and authority – one that poses a threat to our democracy.” She added that France was “caught in a vice – effectively held hostage – between violence and powerlessness”.

Caught between these competing narratives is the centrist bloc of Macron, whose presidency began amid the Yellow Vest protests and is now approaching its end against the backdrop of another major wave of social unrest. That earlier movement, initially triggered by a rise in fuel taxes, grew into a broader revolt against the cost of living and what demonstrators saw as Macron’s favouring of the elite.

One of the differences between now and then is that any government coming next will not have the fiscal room to quell the unrest by handing a cheque. Last year, the government recorded a deficit of 5.1 percent of France’s gross domestic product, one of the highest among European countries. By contrast, the European Union average is 3.1 percent. Any future president will have to deal with Macron’s headache: How to save money without deepening public anger.

The current mobilisation has exposed a wider sense of disillusionment with the political establishment. The president’s popularity stands at 15 percent, the lowest ever.

In his speech on Sunday night, Macron blamed “insurrectionists from fringe far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals” for the violence. But he only briefly spoke about the students’ demands and offered no specific new policy measures to address them. Instead, he tasked Lecornu with bringing together students, teachers, unions and elected officials to develop proposals in the coming days, while promising a tougher response to violence.

The unrest presents an opportunity for his opponents to argue that his presidency has failed to address deep-rooted inequalities. At stake is the support of a generation of young people who feel let down by the state and increasingly disconnected from the political establishment – and who all sides of the political spectrum are poised to woo in the coming months before the election.

articles.title: In the 1970s, California’s Niles Cone groundwater basin needed protection from saltwater intrusion, so a water district began routing creek water into former gravel pits; 13 pits spanning roughly 300 acres now help recharge the aquifer
articles.summary: Discover how California's Alameda County Water District uses former gravel pits to recharge groundwater and protect against saltwater intrusion, ensuring a safe water supply for communities.
articles.body: 13 former gravel pits covered roughly 300 acres in Fremont, California, and now form part of a groundwater recharge system that is operated by the Alameda County Water District (ACWD), which directs water from Alameda Creek into the pits so it can seep underground. The district was working to protect the Niles Cone groundwater basin from saltwater intrusion in the early 1970s, which led to the establishment of the project. The problem was that seawater from San Francisco Bay had entered parts of the freshwater aquifer, which threatened a supply that was used by communities in southern Alameda County, and the district needed to replenish groundwater and limit the movement of saline water into freshwater zones.The current Quarry Lakes system uses water held behind inflatable rubber dams in the Alameda Creek Flood Control Channel, which the district diverts into former gravel quarries, where it percolates through the ground and replenishes the aquifer below. The district had used gravel pits for groundwater recharge since at least the 1930s, but the arrangement of lakes currently and diversion structures dates to the early 1970s.Saltwater intrusion prompted a wider groundwater recovery effortThe district installed its first rubber dam to increase groundwater recharge capacity in 1972, and two years later, it launched an Aquifer Reclamation Program for the specific reason of removing saltwater from the groundwater basin. In 1982, ACWD began drilling a group of wells as part of its Salinity Barrier Program, another measure that was intended to prevent saltwater intrusion, while the district also expanded its recharge infrastructure over time. Its third rubber dam was built in 1989, and it acquired additional recharge pits in 1990 and 1992.The groundwater basin lies beneath Fremont, Newark and Union City, and the ACWD says that it supplies up to half of the water used in those three communities. The district also operates wells that extract groundwater for distribution, and blends it with supplies from the San Francisco Regional Water System.USGS traced how recharge water moves undergroundA US Geological Survey study examined groundwater movement in the Niles Cone and southern East Bay Plain subbasins, where satellite-based measurements, groundwater chemistry and isotope analysis were used to investigate where recharge water travels and how the aquifers may connect. The study found that water entering the ground at Quarry Lakes can affect groundwater pressure as far as about five miles away, near the transition between the Niles Cone and East Bay Plain subbasins, and its influence on water quality was more local, since changes that were associated with recharge were apparent in wells less than two miles from the recharge sources.The researchers also found evidence that water can move through connected aquifers at different depths, since recharge from Quarry Lakes can reach the upper aquifer system at depths that went below 400 feet of the land surface and the deeper aquifer at depths that exceeded 650 feet. The findings also showed that the legacy of earlier saltwater intrusion has not completely disappeared, since parts of the Niles Cone basin still contain groundwater with elevated chloride concentrations that caused saline water to enter before the 1970s. The Quarry Lakes system continues to recharge the basin with water from Alameda Creek, and the former gravel pits now act as both groundwater storage areas and part of a regional recreation area, while the district continues to monitor groundwater quality and manage the risk of saltwater intrusion.You use AI every day. You think Uncle Sam is going to do better? Make housing more affordable? The New Democrat Coalition, a centrist group of legislators, wants to: "Cut red tape and update permitting and zoning to build four million homes in the next decade", sounding a lot like Trump, who has prioritized permitting reform for years. Democrats also promise to protect consumers from price hikes driven by data centers, an issue which should be solved at the local level and not by Washington bureaucrats. The coalition fails to prioritize exploiting America’s enormous reserves of fossil fuels, which over time will guarantee affordable energy. Joe Biden did his best to squash climbing oil and gas production, by canceling or delaying lease sales, drilling permits and the XL Pipeline, raising fees on production and taking promising acreage off the table. The anti-oil war waged by the Biden White House, beholden to the green lobby, was a costly hit to U.S. national security and our economy. Blocking new production, like in Alaska, will inevitably lead to higher oil prices. We cannot let that happen. Yes, we need faster permitting of the build-out of the electric grid, and, yes, we should embrace an "all of the above" energy program. That is not what the Left will allow. Progressives like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani aim to make life more affordable by having the government provide "free" housing, childcare and other services. Meanwhile, government spending on entitlements and benefits has driven our national debt to $40 trillion, pushing interest rates and mortgage costs higher. Under President Joe Biden, spending exploded to levels commensurate with World War II; it remains at unsustainable levels. The Trump White House has put some limits on Medicaid and other expensive programs — limits Democrats will surely race to eliminate — and is trying to root out hundreds of billions in fraudulent payments. Much more needs to be done, but Democrats have zero appetite for cutting spending. articles.title: 'Spend some time with family': Abhijeet Dipke tells 'cockroaches' to not feel weak
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has urged volunteers to spend time with their families during the upcoming festivals, while
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has urged volunteers to spend time with their families during the upcoming festivals, while asking them not to give in to hatred or provocation amid the recent detentions of activists associated with the movement.In a video shared on X, Dipke thanked supporters for standing by one another and said the movement would continue to follow the path of peace, love and compassion. His message came amid the detention of CJP leaders Sourav Das and Ashutosh, whom he described as his brothers.“The past few days have not been easy for us,” Dipke said, recalling his earlier warnings during the movement at Jantar Mantar that the activists could face police action and cases.The video followed Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) Court decision to extend the judicial custody of CJP leaders Saurabh Das and Ashutosh Ranka till October 21. They were produced before the SEM after 5 days of judicial custody on Monday.Dipke, in the video, also acknowledged that several volunteers had allegedly been beaten, detained and subjected to difficulties during detention. However, he said the consequences had also affected their families, who had not chosen to be part of the struggle.“Spend time with your families. Be there with your families, be there with your loved ones,” he urged volunteers, adding that their families would be worried after the events of the past few days.‘We don’t have to become what we hate’Emphasising the need to maintain the movement's commitment to non-violence, Dipke said the difficulties faced by activists should not push them towards hatred.“We are fighting against hatred, we are fighting against the people who have nothing but hatred in their mind. But we also have to ensure that that hatred does not come inside us,” he said.He alleged that the activists were being provoked into abandoning their chosen path of peace and compassion. “We don't have to become what we hate,” he said, reiterating that the movement would not respond to hatred with hatred.Dipke also said emotions should not be mistaken for weakness, describing love, kindness and compassion as the movement's biggest strengths.“Our emotions are not our weakness. They are our strength,” he said.‘We will not back down’Dipke invoked Mahatma Gandhi and BR Ambedkar while describing the values he said should guide the movement. He said the activists' response to their detention reflected their commitment to peaceful resistance.“When Sourav and Ashutosh will come out, they will come out of jail with the slogan of Inquilab Zindabad," he said." I want to add one more thing to this. The people who have been doing this and that in France for the past few days, have some shame. Look at what is happening in India. In India, Sourav Das and Ashutosh went to jail with a smile. They did not do what was happening in France. When they knew they were being put in jail in a wrong way, yet they chose peace."He also appealed to supporters to remember Das and Ashutosh during the festivals, saying the two would be unable to celebrate with their families while in jail.Concluding his message, Dipke thanked volunteers for their support and acknowledged that many had struggled without their experiences receiving public attention.“I know Sourav and Ashu's stories are in the news. My story is in the news. But there are so many volunteers whose story is not in the news but they have struggled as much as Sourav and Ashu,” he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2014, auctioneers uncovered a long-hidden French farm collection that, along with a dirt-covered Ferrari once owned by Alain Delon, sold for €16.288 million in 2015
articles.summary: A hidden collection of classic cars, including a €16.288 million Ferrari once owned by actor Alain Delon, was uncovered in a French farm auction. Discover the cars' remarkable stories and historical significance.
articles.body: A collection of approximately 60 classic cars was found on a farm in western France and fetched a hammer price of €16.288 million at auction in February 2015, according to The Guardian. Among the cars, one stood out: a 1961 Ferrari 250 GT SWB California Spider previously owned by French actor Alain Delon. For decades, the cars had eluded public view, and several of them showed signs of deterioration after spending years in makeshift shelters.The collection came to light in 2014 after Artcurial auctioneers received information about the vehicles, and the property’s exact location was kept confidential by the auction house. The find brought together rare models from manufacturers including Bugatti, Hispano-Suiza, Talbot-Lago, Panhard-Levassor, Maserati, Ferrari, Delahaye and Delage.The discovery and its historical significanceWhile travelling across France in search of rare automotive pieces, Artcurial managing director Matthieu Lamoure and senior specialist Pierre Novikoff received a tip. On pursuing the lead, they visited the farm, which contained different cars, some affected by rust or vegetation, and in certain places corrugated iron rested directly on the cars. For Novikoff, uncovering the collection felt like stepping into a cross between a metallic graveyard and a museum. The auctioneer even compared the find to discovering the tomb of Tutankhamun, underscoring the collection’s exceptional size and the variety of its models.Other cars found on the farm included a Citroën Type C 5 HP Torpedo, a Delahaye 235 coachbuilt by Chapron and a Sandford Type S Cyclecar. The range of manufacturers and vehicle types demonstrated the breadth of the collection, which Artcurial planned to sell in the same condition in which they had been found. King Farouk of Egypt’s Talbot-Lago T26 Cabriolet was also found among the vehicles; he was the country’s last monarch who had developed a reputation for extravagant taste which extended to automobiles. The car’s royal provenance distinguished it from other vehicles in the collection and added another notable historical connection to the discovery. Ultimately, the discovery allowed collectors an opportunity to acquire cars that had spent decades outside the usual classic-car market.The Ferrari's ownership history and auction resultAccording to the Art Hit Parade, the first Ferrari 250 GT SWB California Spider was displayed at the Geneva Motor Show in March 1960 and completed by Scaglietti that May. Later, photographs showed Delon with the Ferrari alongside actresses Jane Fonda and Shirley MacLaine, and by 1964 he took the car to California with his wife, Nathalie.In 1965, Delon sold the Ferrari to Paul Bouvot, the head of Peugeot's styling centre at that time, who retained it for a year before selling it away. After going through several owners, the car was added to the Baillon collection in November 1971, expanding the prestigious collection that his father, Roger Baillon, started in the 1950s.The Artcurial catalogue recorded that the Ferrari’s surviving records included old registration documents and insurance papers which still carried Delon’s name. Another important feature about the car was its production rarity, which made it particularly sought after by collectors. Out of the 52 short-wheelbase California Spiders produced, only 37 were fitted with covered headlights, and this car belonged to that exclusive group. articles.title: ‘There’s a hunger to express yourself’: A dispatch from China’s most fashionable city
articles.summary: Dubbed the “Paris of the East,” Shanghai has long been China’s “most dressed-up city,” according to its thriving community of creatives.
articles.body: One of China’s most exciting art curators, X Zhu-Nowell, is giving me a very Shanghai morning. We share a breakfast of traditional staples –– scallion pancakes, salty bean curd and soup dumplings –– in an Art Deco museum building as she recalls the work of the Chinese American writer Eileen Chang, who was born in 1920s Shanghai. “They’re the first thing that comes to mind,” Zhu-Nowell said of Chang’s vivid descriptions of the cheongsam, or qipao, which often serve as sociological lenses through which we understand her characters –– from how the textiles match, to the fit and even how humidity comes into play. Historically, Shanghai (which birthed the modern qipao) has always been very open to different styles, they added. “People have always been inspired by so much of the landscape and the cityscape, and also the international influence that comes into the city.” I’m in the “Paris of the East” for the tail-end of Shanghai Fashion Week to see what some of China’s most exciting designers are working on today. But I also want to interrogate Shanghai’s style identity, beyond the runways, through the people who live here. “It’s probably China’s most dressed-up city,” said the curator. “The kids are really adventurous with their style, and it’s always personal. Guangzhou people like to wear flip flops. Beijing is very chill.” Zhu-Nowell is executive director and chief curator of Shanghai’s Rockbund Art Museum, which occupies a 1930s building renovated by British architect David Chipperfield in 2010. The five-story brick structure anchors the historic Rockbund neighborhood, a charming area near the iconic Bund riverfront with an impressively high concentration of Art Deco buildings. Blue-chip art galleries, indie boutiques and lifestyle brands –– like Beast, a Chinese perfume maker whose store heaves with floral displays and dispenses perfumes from playful wood-carved animals, and Songmont, which creates architectural, Chinese heritage-inspired bags. A collision of art and architecture, the area has also become a photogenic backdrop for fashion lovers. By around 9 a.m., I’d seen over a dozen photo shoots taking place – a bride-to-be in a strapless wedding dress and knee-high boots; a 20-something aspiring model in a white winter puffer posing for a Taobao store ad; a woman embracing Old Shanghai-style glamour with finger-wave curls and a green floral qipao; and a gaggle of well-turned-out grannies striking poses. “The children have grown up, and now we’re enjoying our lives into old age, but our hearts are young,” said one of them, 69-year-old Didi. She humbly described her style as “sui yi,” or very “whatever,” though it seemed anything but. “Shanghai is more forward when it comes to fashion, it’s true. I like to look cleaner… more put together.” Waiting to get into Mark Gong’s Shanghai Fashion Week show, I stood beside Abigail Man, a 30-year-old influencer styled in a sheer, lacy, high-necked top and leopard-print jeans (both by the designer’s eponymous brand). I’d seen her earlier that day at Samuel Guì Yang’s show, where she stood out from the crowd thanks to both her striking bob, reminiscent of Japanese anime character Paprika, and her unexpected pairing of a loose-fitting poppy-motif tunic with the label’s Adidas collaboration track pants. Man told me she moved to Shanghai after years in New York and Dalian, her hometown in northeastern China. She liked it here because the people are “willing to look bolder, compared to other places.” Shanghai, and China as a whole, has become turbo-charged and hyper modern with high tech infrastructure and AI. The city itself felt largely quiet with the hum of so many electric vehicles. No one uses cash, everything is on an app, everything can be bought at lighting speed. That speed contributes to a palpable sense of possibility. Landon Du, the project director of Shanghai Fashion Week’s organizing committee, talked about how compared to style capitals like Milan and Paris, and their heritage brands, in China: “Fashion is young. Brands are young. Designers are young. The audience is young.” Samuel Guì Yang, who showed off-schedule at another 1930s venue, epitomizes what many young people in today’s China desire: reinterpreting and bringing traditional Chinese aesthetics into design. For that, the work by him and co-founder Erit Litzén, who met at London’s Central Saint Martins, is often categorized as “new Chinese style.” They don’t necessarily identify with the label that is often thrust upon them –– as they’ve long merged Eastern and Western visual codes –– but the pair recognize they’re part of a wider movement built around China’s growing cultural confidence. “There’s an energy, a hunger, and a will to express yourself here,” said Litzén. “Not just in Shanghai, but in China. There’s a huge surge of people who want to explore fashion and culture in a broader sense. It’s really fertile ground for young businesses.” Based in both London and Shanghai, Samuel Guì Yang has opened its first physical store last weekend. The label chose a spot on Julu Road, a popular tree-lined street in Shanghai’s former French quarter packed with little boutiques and independent Chinese designers. Outside one of its cafes I find 30-year-old Ma Xue Li, who is visiting from nearby Zhejiang province to work at the Rolex Shanghai Masters tennis tournament. She’s tucking into a good-looking slice of cheesecake and sitting next to her friend’s equally good-looking dog (in a yellow pastel vest embroidered with flowers and a ruffled white trim). “It’s daring, its fearless,” she observes of how people in Shanghai dress. “More importantly, it’s a way of life where you don’t have to fit into certain social norms or expectations.” Osschaert, one of the event’s last shows, took me by surprise. Designer duo Kong Yue and Xie Yonghao eschewed a traditional runway for a poignant, at times unsettling theater presentation about memory and loss, with the actors mostly in white garment prototypes, before eventually appearing together in their finalized, ethereal forms. It appeared to resonate with the crowd. Richard Chan, who heads product development and design at Disney’s fashion department in Shanghai, said he felt the show represented how Chinese brands are increasingly connecting with people through storytelling, not just clothes. More broadly, Chan said, “there’s a big shift in the way people have chosen to exercise their creativity in society.” “It can be across food, clothing, the way people enjoy tourism,” he said, pointing to barbecue street snacks that can now be had in bright, glamorous eateries, or the new bars that serve cocktails based on ingredients used in traditional Chinese medicine. “Everything becomes more authentically Chinese, but through the lens of the modern world.” Scroll down for some of shows from Shanghai Fashion Week. Shanghai Fashion Week featured over 80 runways shows and presentations. Du, the project director of its organizing committee, said that over the past decade, Chinese labels have developed “stronger brand DNA.” “I think in the past, when Chinese designers graduated from Western design schools, they followed trends. But now when they do their own collections, they have more self-expression… which makes them more distinctive,” he said, speaking after the Shuting Qiu runway. “In recent years, they will incorporate more Chinese identity and elements in their designs, in a modern and contemporary way.” Designer Mark Gong, worn by the likes of Rihanna, Charli XCX and Jennie, put on a romantic show. The skirts were super flirty and bounced a lot and everyone in the audience looked hot. Samuel Guì Yang’s latest collection is named after, and inspired by, the 1990s Hong Kong film “Green Snake,” starring Maggie Cheung. They were both figurative and literal references to the animal, with snakeskin patterns and fabrics that moved as if they were slithering. A painting of tides by Southern Song dynasty painter Ma Yuan influenced the collection’s notions of water and fluidity. The designers spoke about “feeding themselves” with inspiration from Shanghai by going to old bookshops, the parks and ghost markets. Models literally ran down the catwalk at times during Adidas’ high-octane show with multiple acts. Singer Veegee wore a voluminous skirt layered with cuts of tracksuits and flannel during one performance. The event, held at the ROJO Art Space, included exhibition-like experiences and a tennis court. It’s all in the details. Even the mini bamboo baskets serving up little delicacies before the show bore the brand’s signature three stripes. At Osschaert, the audience was transported to a forest with leaves scattered on the ground and turf, entering a dream-like set that centered around a young, aspiring designer’s workshop. One by one, her cohorts are led away by a ghostly figure, who says, “When time is up, I appear.” A parade of nerdy chic models strutted down the Shushu/Tong runway. I was obsessed with the girly girl vibe struck by the brand’s new collection. It’s giving quasi-nerd who loves a little retro styling and a cute bubble skirt. Backstage at Youtopia, I spoke with Tasha Liu, a leader on the Shanghai fashion scene for co-founding Labelhood, an incubator for Chinese brands, that also helped to stage shows like Mark Gong and Shushu/Tong during the event. Youtopia platformed the work of emerging Chinese designers, many recent graduates. “More and more designers will focus on their own culture,” Liu said. “They will be true to themselves.” At the finale, models walked down with boxes for audiences to cast votes for their favorite look.

articles.title: Michael Robinson accused Jalen Hurts of faking an injury — then doctors found clots in his lungs
articles.summary: Michael Robinson suggested on NFL Network that Jalen Hurts was faking his injury, but doctors then found blood clots in the Eagles QB's lungs.
articles.body: The question during Monday's OutKick meeting went as follows: Did Michael Robinson just give the worst-aged sports take in history? It happened Thursday on NFL Network, when the former fullback suggested that Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts was faking an injury so as not to be the fall guy for a losing team. "He's pulling himself out, so this doesn't look like it's on me," Robinson said. EAGLES QUARTERBACK JALEN HURTS RULED OUT OF SUNDAY'S GAME 'OUT OF AN ABUNDANCE OF CAUTION' DUE TO BLOOD CLOT On October 4, Hurts was cleated in the calf against the Rams. Six days later, an ultrasound revealed a superficial blood clot. He still played against the Jaguars the following day in London, despite doctors reportedly keeping him awake all night over concerns about the risks associated with sleeping with a blood clot. On October 15, the Eagles released a statement saying Hurts wouldn't play Sunday against the Panthers. That night, Robinson chucked his now-infamous verbal air ball. "If I'm Jalen Hurts or anybody in the Jalen Hurts' camp, I'm saying 'if everybody is hurt, then I'm hurt, too'," he said, referring to the rash of injuries on the Eagles roster. Robinson added: "I would advise all of our viewers to go Google 'superficial blood clot' as opposed to a real blood clot." EAGLES APPEAR SET TO ADD QB FROM COWBOYS' PRACTICE SQUAD AS JALEN HURTS DEALS WITH BLOOD CLOT Well, it turns out Hurts' condition was far more serious than Robinson suggested. Doctors subsequently discovered blood clots in his lungs — and now he's expected to miss the rest of the season. Part of me wondered if Robinson's season as a broadcaster was in jeopardy as well, although he did issue the following apology Monday night." "I want to sincerely apologize to Jalen Hurts, his family, the Philadelphia Eagles organization and fan base for my comments last Thursday. They were unfounded and I never should've speculated on a health issue of a player nor his commitment to this team." The mea culpa seems sincere — and boy was it necessary. I will admit that my favorite key on my laptop is delete. It's rare that I have to come up with an opinion on a hot mic. But to imply that a world-class athlete is exaggerating an injury to preserve his reputation is a staggering lapse in judgment. On the off chance that Robinson was correct, he might have scored a day-long victory lap. But whiffing like that gave his credibility a permanent stain. NBA GREAT SAYS HE NEARLY 'DROPPED DEAD' DUE TO BLOOD CLOT AS HE OFFERS ADVICE TO VICTOR WEMBANYAMA THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Don't get me wrong, there have been a lot of bad sports opinions that had little impact on the pundit's career. In 2016, Max Kellerman said that Tom Brady was about to "fall off a cliff," only to watch the QB win three more Super Bowls. In 2014, Skip Bayless said that Johnny Manziel was going to be bigger in Cleveland than LeBron James ever was. In 2010, Mel Kiper Jr. said he would retire from ESPN if Jimmy Clausen — who went 1-13 in the 14 NFL games he started — was not a successful quarterback. And last month, LA Times columnist Bill Plaschke said that this year's Rams would go undefeated en route to the Super Bowl (they are 2-4). But none of those takes attacked a man's character the way Robinson attacked Hurts'. They might have been ridiculous, but they were also harmless. Look, I don't want to see Robinson lose his gig the way some online angry villagers do. He gave an egregious opinion, but one reckless remark shouldn't erase a career's worth of work. articles.title: Some synagogues canceled prayers as French Jews faced warnings amid violent protests
articles.summary: Some French Jews reportedly faced unprecedented warnings to hide their identity as anti-government protests turned violent across the nation.
articles.body: For some French Jews, Saturday's unrest brought an unsettling warning: conceal outward signs of Jewish identity and avoid gathering outside synagogues. One community member told Fox News Digital that some congregations had even canceled afternoon prayers on the Sabbath as demonstrations across France descended into violence. Ahead of the protests on Saturday, he said, as a precaution, "Lots of synagogues sent out emails to their people saying, 'We're canceling Mincha on Shabbat afternoon. Please don't go out. It's going to be dangerous,'" Samuel Arrouas, a French Jewish community member who divides his time between Paris and Israel, told Fox News Digital. Mincha is the Jewish afternoon prayer service. Arrouas, who returned to Israel before Saturday's protests, described his shock over the messages. "I'm 40 years old. First time I heard this," he said. FRANCE'S MASSIVE INTEL FAILURE SPARKS RESIGNATION OFFERS AMID DAYS OF RIOTING Arrouas said warnings also advised Jews against visibly wearing kippahs, traditional skullcaps, or tzitzit, ritual fringes worn by observant Jewish men. Worshipers were discouraged from lingering outside synagogues after services. "You go to prayers, and you immediately leave," he said. Before leaving France, Arrouas said he encountered masked demonstrators carrying Palestinian flags near Paris Dauphine University. "It's very scary," he said. "When you're Jewish and you pass in front of such a scene, the only thing you want to do is just get away." The concerns emerged as approximately 550,000 people demonstrated across France on Oct. 17 against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. The demonstrations were masked rioters clashed with police, looted businesses and set fire to vehicles and buildings in Paris, Marseille and other cities. France's Interior Ministry reported approximately 2,400 arrests. ISRAELI AMBASSADOR COMPARES FRANCE'S FAR-LEFT LEADER'S RHETORIC TO HITLER AS ANTISEMITISM SURGES President Emmanuel Macron called for "calm and order" in a national address, warning against escalation. "We all feel anger and shame," he said, distinguishing protesters' "legitimate demands" from "those who destroyed, smashed and looted." He said "nothing justifies" the violence and pledged accountability. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation, which Macron refused. Shannon Seban, the France-based executive director of European affairs at the Combat Antisemitism Movement, said the presence of Palestinian flags at demonstrations over domestic issues added to Jewish community concerns. "We have seen Palestinian flags at demonstrations that were supposed to be about education and social demands. What does Gaza have to do with any of this?" Seban told Fox News Digital. INSIDE THE PROTEST PLAYBOOK TO VILIFY ISRAEL ON 'GLOBAL DAY OF ACTION' "This has nothing to do with legitimate student demands anymore. We are talking about organized violence, about people who are not coming to demonstrate but to destroy, to attack our police officers and to challenge the authority of the Republic," she said. Seban linked the violence to rhetoric urging people to "globalize the intifada" and to antisemitic conspiracy theories circulating online. "At the Combat Antisemitism Movement, we documented 1,384 antisemitic posts in just two days, including conspiracy theories accusing Jews and Israel of being behind the unrest," Seban said. "The right to protest is fundamental in a democracy. But the right to protest is not the right to destroy," she added. "France and Europe must wake up. Before it is too late." In Marseille, Bruno Benjamin, president of the Marseille-Provence branch of CRIF, the Representative Council of French Jewish Institutions, described the damage to local businesses and the anxiety facing the community. "Several hundred shops were ransacked, vandalized and looted. The scale of the devastation is simply unbearable," Benjamin told Fox News Digital. He said shopkeepers had seen years of work destroyed within hours, leaving some facing layoffs or temporary unemployment for employees. "This is not just an attack on businesses. It is an attack on people's livelihood, their dignity, and the very fabric of our society," he said. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER France's Jewish community security organization, SPCJ, cautioned against assuming that Jewish-owned property was targeted because of religion. In a statement provided to Fox News Digital, SPCJ said a break-in and vandalism at a synagogue in Paris's 19th arrondissement initially suggested burglary, although the motive remained undetermined. Jewish-owned businesses were among those damaged in Marseille, it said, without evidence they had been singled out for being Jewish. The U.S. State Department's existing Level 2 travel advisory urges Americans to exercise increased caution in France because of terrorism and unrest. Fox News Digital reached out to the French Embassy in Washington, D.C., for comment on the unrest and the safety of the Jewish community. Benjamin said rising insecurity and antisemitism had left some French Jews considering whether to leave the country, while others remained determined to stay. articles.title: Lawmaker reportedly loses leg as car ramming stuns Australia
articles.summary: An Australian lawmaker was in critical but stable condition Tuesday after being hit by a car in what authorities said was a deliberate attack, shocking a nation where political violence is extremely rare.
articles.body: An Australian lawmaker was in critical but stable condition Tuesday after being hit by a car in what authorities said was a deliberate attack, shocking a nation where political violence is extremely rare. Helen Haines, a 65-year-old independent member of Parliament, was struck Monday by a white Toyota Land Cruiser outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta, a town of about 30,000 people in the southern Australian state of Victoria. She underwent surgery overnight after being airlifted to a hospital in the state capital of Melbourne, about 150 miles away. Local media reported that one of Haines’s legs had been amputated and that she was fighting to keep her other leg. The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne did not respond to an NBC News request for comment on the reports. Police charged the driver, who they said was a 43-year-old local man, on Tuesday with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said earlier Tuesday that according to eyewitnesses, the driver had passed Haines and then performed a U-turn, hitting her as she was standing by the trunk of her parked car. “It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone, you know, just skidding off the road,” he told the Australian Broadcasting Corp., adding that the motivation was not yet clear. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told the ABC that witnesses had described seeing the driver reverse and then hit Haines a second time. The suspect’s father said the family knew Haines well. She was a “deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community,” Brendan Nugent’s father Rod Nugent and Rod’s partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement Tuesday. “Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” the statement added. Political violence is extremely rare in Australia, where lawmakers are often out in public with little or no security and their accessibility is a point of national pride. “It’s an Australian tradition to have a chat to a politician that you bump into at the shops,” Josh Roose, an associate professor of politics at Deakin University in Melbourne, told NBC News in an interview. But threats are rising as political rhetoric becomes more extreme, officials and experts say, particularly since the Covid-19 pandemic. According to the Australian Federal Police, there were 1,067 incidents of threats, harassment, nuisance or offensive behavior against senior officeholders, parliamentarians and protected locations in the 2025-26 financial year, a 12% increase over the previous year and twice the number five years earlier. In a 2023 study of Victoria state parliamentarians, 82% reported harassment and 85% reported threats of harm, said Josh Holloway, a senior lecturer in government at Flinders University in Adelaide, with female politicians more likely to face abuse. Holloway said that Australian federal lawmakers, especially those in rural areas, typically work from “shopfront-style offices,” hold regular community meetings and attend local events without security. Those practices may now come under scrutiny, “but reducing public access to their representatives can come with significant democratic cost,” he said in emailed comments. Albanese said Tuesday that it was everyone’s responsibility to “turn the temperature down.” “We can disagree with each other, but do it in a respectful way,” he told Australia’s “Today” show. “And that’s something that Helen Haines always was characterized by, was that respect that she showed to others right across the political spectrum.” Albanese said later that he had spoken by phone with local barber Ricky Jefferies, who ran from his nearby shop to help detain Haines’s attacker in what Albanese said was “a great example of the Australian spirit.” “I heard a loud bang, with no brakes. It was crazy,” Jefferies told reporters. “I just ran out the front to see what was happening.” Jefferies, who said he removed a knife from the suspect’s pocket and pulled him out of the car, said a lot of people “just ran to help.” Haines, a mother and grandmother who spent three decades working in rural health as a nurse and midwife and has a doctorate in childbirth, was first elected to Parliament in 2019, then re-elected in 2022 and 2025. Her family said in a statement that they were grateful for the “swift assistance of bystanders” as well as first responders. The increase in political threats in Australia follows a similar trend in the United States and other liberal democracies, Roose said. “Australia always echoes what we’re seeing internationally, but sometimes slightly behind,” he said. Since the Covid-19 pandemic, there has emerged a “level of extremist discourse that is unparalleled in Australian history,” Roose said, one that is highly influenced by politics in the U.S. Australia, and particularly Victoria, had some of the strictest pandemic lockdowns in the world, which left residents feeling “imprisoned, but also disempowered,” he said. Lingering feelings of resentment combined with the current high cost of housing, fuel and other necessities have contributed to a “deep hostility” toward the government, Roose said. Politics in rural Australia, especially, have become “highly inflammatory,” he said, “because of the online space and the poverty and the desperation that, quite frankly, has seeped into these areas.” Roose said the “paradox” was that the victim was Haines, who is not considered a polarizing figure and is “someone who’s grown up and spent most of their life in these regions.” “It indicates, I suppose, the challenge facing democracies around the world,” he said.

articles.title: Martha's Vineyard police barracks rocked after woman 'ran for her life,' found naked outside: prosecutor
articles.summary: Edward Brown allegedly met the victim at a bar in Oak Bluffs before prosecutors say the attack occurred inside the Martha's Vineyard barracks.
articles.body: A school security official at an elite Boston school has been charged with the rape of a woman visiting from Ireland after police say they found her naked on the side of the road outside the Massachusetts State Police barracks on Martha's Vineyard. The suspect was allegedly a guest at the barracks visiting a state trooper friend from college, prosecutors said in court at his arraignment. Edward Brown, 27, pleaded not guilty in connection with the alleged Aug. 15 attack, which prosecutors said took place inside the barracks. 'JAWS' CHILD STAR SWORN IN AS POLICE CHIEF ON MARTHA'S VINEYARD Police say they received two 911 calls around 1 a.m. and arrived to find a naked woman in distress. She told police she ran down two flights of stairs and out of the building and had been on the road for a few minutes before someone stopped to help. The responding Oak Bluffs police officers saw bruises on her legs and a red mark on her neck, Scalice said. The bouncer didn't know his name but knew he was friends with state troopers and had a photo. Oak Bluffs police sent the picture to Costello on Aug. 29, two weeks after the alleged assault, Scalice said. He identified the man shown as Brown and said they'd been friends since college. Then on Sept. 11, Costello's attorney gave investigators screenshots of a text conversation between the trooper and Brown, Scalice said. "Prior to September 11, 2026, these messages had never been provided to any member of law enforcement investigating the alleged rape," Scalice said. Brown allegedly gave shifting accounts of the night to Costello, Scalice told the judge: First he denied bringing a female to the barracks, then he said she'd come inside but left on her own, and then he claimed he left her in the Uber and she never came in. At one point, he allegedly texted Costello, "I'm at the barracks with this chick, is that okay?" Costello, who prosecutors said was not there at the time, replied, "okay." Brown then allegedly asked him where to find condoms and added, "Beers after I slam." Once detectives identified a suspect and obtained a search warrant for Brown's Uber account, detectives also found a ride from about a half hour before the 911 calls. "Officers interviewed the Uber driver who confirmed picking up a Black male matching the defendant's description and a very young looking White female and driving them to the State Police barracks," Scalice said. "The Uber driver described the female as appearing very intoxicated while the Black male was not." Brown is listed in jail records as 5 feet, 11 inches tall and 260 pounds. Prosecutors said that they learned from Boston police that he had been the subject of four police reports from two ex-girlfriends claiming he had been harassing them between March and August of this year. Oak Bluffs police, working with the Boston Police Department's anti-corruption division, arrested Brown at Boston Latin Academy, where he worked in school security, on Oct. 9. Police allegedly found suspected cocaine in his wallet during the arrest. "The Massachusetts State Police has had no involvement in the Oak Bluffs Police Department’s investigation," Oak Bluffs Police Chief Jonathan Searle said in a Sept. 10 statement, a month before Brown's arrest. "As part of its investigation, Oak Bluffs Police developed probable cause and applied for and received court-authorized search warrants related to the investigation, including warrants executed at the State Police barracks." articles.title: After paying Rs 29,500 for a family cruise, a Kerala SBI manager travelled from Thiruvananthapuram to Kochi, only to find the trip cancelled without notice; consumer commission orders Rs 54,500 payout plus interest
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Kerala has held a holiday company and a cruise operator guilty of deficiency in service after a family
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Kerala has held a holiday company and a cruise operator guilty of deficiency in service after a family reached Kochi for a booked cruise trip only to learn that it had been cancelled without prior notice.The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kannur, directed Plumeria Holidays, its managing director Aneesh Susheel and Nefertiti Sea Cruise to jointly and severally refund Rs 29,500 with interest, pay Rs 15,000 as compensation and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs, in its order dated October 9, 2026.Cruise trip cancellation disputeAccording to the commission order, the complainant, Jayakrishnan P, chief manager at the State Bank of India’s Thiruvananthapuram branch, had paid Rs 29,500 for a prepaid holiday plan offered by Plumeria Holidays. The plan, called Plumeria Black, included hotel stays, dinner buffets and four Nefertiti cruise trips.The complainant booked a cruise trip for September 6, 2024, and travelled with his family from Thiruvananthapuram to Kochi after taking leave from work. A room at Avenue Regent hotel had also been arranged under the package. However, when the family reached the cruise departure point before the scheduled time, they were informed that the trip had been cancelled.He alleged that the cruise management behaved rudely towards the family and that he was not informed of the cancellation in advance. He said he repeatedly sought a refund of the booking amount, but the opposite parties did not return it. He approached the commission seeking a refund of Rs 29,500, Rs 50,000 as compensation, Rs 25,000 for leave and travel expenses, and litigation costs.Plumeria Holidays and Aneesh Susheel argued that the cruise had been cancelled because of a technical issue and that they learnt of the cancellation only when the complainant informed them. They said the cruise ticket charges would be returned to his prepaid card and that he could use the remaining services under the plan.Nefertiti Sea Cruise said the trip had been cancelled because of a delay in the issuance of a mandatory Mercantile Marine Department certificate required to operate the cruise. It claimed that it had informed Plumeria Holidays and Aneesh Susheel about the cancellation, and argued that the ticket terms allowed cancellation due to technical or statutory issues and made the ticket fare non-refundable.Commission's finding on cruise cancellationThe bench comprising president Ravi Susha and members Moly Kutty Mathew and Sajeesh K P found that all three opposite parties were responsible for the failure to inform the complainant about the cancellation and the resulting inconvenience.The commission noted that the Mercantile Marine Department certificate was issued on September 7, 2024, a day after the scheduled cruise. It observed that the cruise could not operate without the certificate and that the operator knew permission for the scheduled trip could not be obtained.The commission found that Nefertiti Sea Cruise had failed to produce evidence to establish its claim that it had informed the holiday company in advance. It said the cruise operator could have informed either the holiday company or the complainant about the delay in obtaining permission.The commission also held that Plumeria Holidays and Aneesh Susheel could not avoid responsibility by claiming that they learnt of the cancellation only from the complainant. It noted that the organisers were responsible for obtaining information from the cruise operator and communicating changes to customers.“As the organisers responsible for the trip, OPs 1 and 2 had a duty to obtain the necessary information from OP No. 3 in advance and communicate the same to the customers.”The commission said the non-refund condition in the cruise ticket did not absolve the opposite parties of their responsibility for failing to arrange the trip properly and inform the complainant in advance.“So there is gross deficiency in service on the part of OPs 1 to 3.”It further observed, “Considering the facts and circumstances of this case, there is deficiency in service on the part of OPs1 to 3. So complainant is entitled to get relief from OPs1 to 3.”The commission partly allowed the complaint, holding all three opposite parties liable for the service deficiency.Final orderThe commission, in its October 9, 2026, order, directed the three opposite parties jointly and severally to:Refund the booking amount of Rs 29,500 with 4 percent interest from August 19, 2024, until realisation.Pay Rs 15,000 as compensation.Pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation expenses.Comply with the order within one month of receiving its certified copy.The total amount payable before interest is Rs 54,500. If the opposite parties fail to comply within the specified period, the Rs 29,500 refund and Rs 15,000 compensation will carry interest at 9 percent per annum from the date of the complaint until realisation. The complainant can also seek execution of the order under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

articles.title: Zelenskyy to hold talks on Russia-Ukraine war with Witkoff, Europeans
articles.summary: The prime ministers of Norway and Finland will also attend the discussions in Oslo.
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is set to hold talks with United States special envoy Steve Witkoff and European leaders in Norway, aimed at ending the war with Russia.

The prime ministers of Norway and Finland will attend the talks in Oslo on Tuesday, while President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner is expected to attend remotely because of illness.

The meeting comes as Trump continues to publicly castigate Zelenskyy, accusing him of not wanting to end the war and suggesting that someone else should negotiate on Kyiv’s behalf.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said Zelenskyy requested that Witkoff and Kushner participate in Tuesday’s discussions.

In a post on X before the talks, Zelenskyy said he had engaged in a “substantive conversation” with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio about missile interceptors, intelligence sharing and Starlink, a satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

Last week, Zelenskyy accused Washington of withholding intelligence from Kyiv and limiting Starlink’s internet speed. Ukraine’s armed forces use SpaceX’s military-grade internet network Starshield for several operations, including drone attacks.

Zelenskyy did not confirm whether Rubio had committed to addressing the issues raised, including supplying Ukraine with crucial US-made Patriot missile interceptors and restoring intelligence sharing and Starshield services. However, he described the discussion as “constructive” and said the two had agreed to speak again soon.

The talks come as the two warring sides continue to launch long-range air attacks on each other.

At least three people were killed across Ukraine in Russian attacks on Tuesday. A Russian drone struck a highway connecting Kyiv to the Black Sea port of Odesa, killing three people and injuring four, Kyiv’s regional prosecutor’s office confirmed.

Meanwhile, more than 32,000 families are without electricity after Ukraine’s largest private energy company, DTEK, confirmed that three of its energy facilities in the southern Odesa region had been hit by Russia.

The governor of Russia’s Tambov Oblast said on Tuesday that a fire had broken out at an oil pumping station after an overnight Ukrainian drone attack. Yevgeny Pervyshov said four drones were intercepted.

Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, while easing pressure on Russia, including lifting sanctions on its diesel exports. Trump has been eager to bring down energy prices, which have surged as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran.

Zelenskyy has described the agreement to waive sanctions on Russian diesel as a “reward” for President Vladimir Putin, warning that it would only embolden him.
