articles.title: Florida is set to carry out 18th execution this year and moving closer to tying record
articles.summary: MIAMI — Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov.
articles.body: MIAMI — Florida is set Tuesday to carry out its 18th execution of the year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves, 77, was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski. He would become Florida’s eighth prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, which has highlighted the nation's aging death-row population and underscored how Florida has outpaced the rest of the country in executions. Reaves was set to receive a three-drug injection starting at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out. Fought with a deputy after dropping a gun According to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful. The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida's method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution. Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. Supreme Court. Florida is close to matching last year's record-setting numbers A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 31 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. 5. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

articles.title: US leaving oil-for-security approach, not Middle East: Envoy Tom Barrack
articles.summary: Barrack highlights limits of US interventions, admitting past regime changes in the Middle East were often mistakes.
articles.body:
Doha, Qatar — The United States is moving away from its traditional security-for-oil relationship with the Middle East and no longer seeks to dominate the region, senior US diplomat Tom Barrack has said.

However, it was not abandoning the Middle East, he added, speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha on Tuesday — but rather reassessing its role, after years of attempts to reshape governments across the region.

“The US no longer wants to own,” said Barrack, who serves as US Ambassador to Turkiye and Special Envoy for Syria. “The bargain is not to control, but to not leave. We’re not leaving.”

Barrack acknowledged that regional countries were increasingly recognising the limits of US involvement.

“Everybody is saying: OK, I can’t rely on America to solve all my problems,” he said.

Barrack questioned the effectiveness of previous interventions, saying that the US had been involved in 23 regime changes across the wider Middle East.

“Every time we try and intervene, change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake,” he said.

His comments come as Washington and Tehran try to negotiate an end to the US-Israeli war on Iran that has destabilised the region and disrupted global energy supplies.

Political analyst Luciano Zaccara described Barrack as probably “the most realistic of Trump’s allies” in his assessment of US involvement in the Middle East.

He told Al Jazeera that Barrack had effectively acknowledged that regime change, one of Trump’s stated objectives in the war on Iran, was unlikely to succeed.

Zaccara said Barrack’s reference to regime changes in the Middle East was an acknowledgement “that what the US has been doing in the region has not been working, regardless of which administration it was”.

According to Zaccara, Barrack had stopped just short of suggesting that Trump needed to retreat from “the maximalist demands” he had made of Iran.

Qatar says negotiations between Tehran and Washington are continuing despite growing fears of renewed fighting.

Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Majed al-Ansari, speaking separately at the Global Security Forum, said mediators were continuing to exchange messages between the warring parties, with regional partners involved in efforts to reach a deal.

“We are working between the parties, continuing our job as mediator with our partners and others in the region,” he said.

Al-Ansari said the lack of public information about the negotiations should not be interpreted as a lack of progress.

“The fact that we’re not hearing about it is a good sign that we’re doing our job properly,” he said.

The diplomatic efforts come as Iran’s seven-day proposal to end the war remains on the table, with the US yet to give its response.

The plan envisages reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear negotiations in exchange for US concessions, including lifting the naval blockade on Iranian ports and easing economic sanctions on Tehran.

Analyst Negar Mortazavi said the diplomatic door remained open, but negotiations were stalled over the terms and sequencing of an agreement.

“Tehran wants to end the war, but it is not prepared to surrender under military or economic pressure,” she told Al Jazeera on the sidelines of the forum in Doha.

The Strait of Hormuz remains a major flashpoint, with attacks on commercial shipping raising concerns over global energy supplies. Before the US-Israeli war on Iran, one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas supplies transited through the strait.

Mortazavi said the escalation was part of Tehran’s strategy to maintain leverage against Washington despite its military disadvantages.

“Iran’s leverage has diminished but has not disappeared,” she said. “Moving tankers is not the same as restoring safe, predictable and normal maritime traffic.”

According to Mortazavi, Tehran wants to increase the economic and political costs of the war for Trump, while signalling to future US administrations that military action against Iran carries consequences.

But she warned that continued escalation posed serious risks to Iran and the wider region.

“Ultimately, neither military escalation nor economic pressure is likely to produce Iranian capitulation,” she said.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson also reaffirmed Doha’s support for Riyadh in the fighting against Yemen’s Houthi armed group, saying it backed Saudi Arabia in “defending their sovereignty against this attack”.

Fighting intensified in September after the Houthis seized areas along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the port city of Mocha. In response, forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched an offensive, dubbed “Dawn of Yemen”, on October 4, backed by Saudi air strikes.

The Houthis have retaliated with missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and military installations. Strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport earlier this month killed at least 14 people and wounded hundreds.

articles.title: Woman describes alleged assault by Russell Brand as 'frenzied' and 'violent'
articles.summary: The entertainer denies three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.
articles.body:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who claims Russell Brand sexually assaulted her has described the alleged attack as "frenzied" and "violent".

Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

On Tuesday, the jury heard from the fourth complainant in the trial, who alleges Brand sexually assaulted her at the Choice FM radio studios in central London in the mid-2000s.

She said she came out of a small room in the building to find Brand outside.

"He said 'aye aye'," she told the jury, "he grabbed me by my face, started to kiss me, and when he was kissing me he started pushing me - his body against me."

The woman continued: "He was kissing me, it was very frenzied. There was no time for me to even understand what was going on.

"He was running his hands over my body and I had my back against the wall at that point."

From behind a blue screen, the woman described the kiss as "sloppy" and "very, very rough", when asked by the prosecution barrister about the alleged attack.

"His hands at the same time were all over me," she said. "He touched my bum, my breasts, his body was pressed up against me."

The woman said she pushed him off and swore at him.

She said there were several people with him who she claims didn't say anything about what happened after the alleged assault.

The woman - now in her 50s - said she had never met Brand before and that she believed he'd been in the building because he was on Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth.

She told the jury: "His whole body was pressed against me - the kisses were hard and sloppy and going down my neck.

"His hands were moving so much - the reason I used the word frenzied was because it was violent. He just wasn't stopping."

Said she felt "dirty" after the encounter and "never told anybody", adding: "I felt shocked and stunned, shaken."

When questioned by Brand's barrister on why none of the people who may have seen what happened raised concerns, the woman said: "It was not the present-day environment."

"On the day it happened - and I ask myself this question - why I didn't share it," she said. "It wasn't the culture where something happened to you and you tell people."

Asked by the defence barrister why she did not go to the police, the woman said: "I would have thought about a few things. Who would have believed me?

"I could lose my job and I had a mortgage to pay," she said, adding that she "buried it for so long".

The woman said she came forward with the allegation after watching a documentary on television about the TV star and his alleged behaviour.

Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

articles.title: 'We're going to die': Passengers recount midair terror before emergency landing
articles.summary: Oxygen masks dropped mid-flight as an American Airlines plane made an emergency landing at St. Louis airport on Oct. 17 after passengers reported a strange odor.
articles.body: A passenger flight was forced to make an emergency landing shortly after takeoff following reports of a strange odor on board that left travelers fearing for their lives. An American Airlines flight departed from St. Louis Lambert International Airport on Oct. 17, bound for Philadelphia, before turning back to the airport. Gary Leff, a Texas-based aviation expert who founded the blog "View from the Wing," told Fox News Digital that engine oil entering an aircraft's air supply could potentially explain the odor, although the cause of the incident has not yet been confirmed. PROBE UNDERWAY AS 7 FLIGHT ATTENDANTS SICKENED BY BAFFLING ODOR ON MAJOR AIRLINE "When that happens, you can get smoke, you can get vibration, you can get loud noises. It can also wind up making people ill," Leff said. FlightAware data reviewed by Fox News Digital showed that the plane was in the air for 34 minutes before landing back at St. Louis Lambert International Airport. In a statement to Fox News Digital, American Airlines confirmed that the flight returned to St. Louis shortly after takeoff following a reported odor on board. The airline said the aircraft landed safely and was taken out of service for inspection by its maintenance team. The flight had already been delayed roughly two hours following a reported engine issue before passengers experienced trouble in the air, according to a couple who spoke to local outlet First Alert 4. TRAVEL NIGHTMARE UNFOLDS AS MAJOR AIRLINE SCRAPS FLIGHT AFTER HARROWING 12-HOUR DELAY The passengers — Tessa and Mark Springer of Waterloo, Illinois — were traveling to Pennsylvania for work when they heard a troubling noise coming from the back of the plane before takeoff. "We heard just this really horrible noise coming from the back of the plane. It was like ... real loud buzzing, kind of [a] grinding sound," Mark Springer said. Mark Springer said the pilot then announced there was a mechanical issue. "The pilot comes back on and says, ‘Uh, there’s a problem with the engine on the airplane,’" the passenger added. "'We can’t get it started.'" 'WE THOUGHT WE WOULD DIE': PASSENGERS THROWN INTO CEILING DURING TERRIFYING FLIGHT After the delay, the plane finally departed. But about 15 minutes into the flight, passengers experienced a sudden jolt that sent them lunging forward, according to Mark Springer. "All of a sudden, the plane just felt like it hit a ... like in a car, when you slam on your brakes. ... Everybody kind of lunges forward like this," he said. "I was like, We’re going to die." "And then, maybe a minute later, the plane just kind of goes boom and drops. … All of the oxygen masks fall. And we just kind of looked at each other like, is this serious? Is this real?" added Mark Springer. Tessa Springer recalled fearing for her life as the plane turned back toward the airport, telling First Alert 4 she was terrified she would die. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER She texted her children, "Problem on our plane, love you guys," per the outlet. "I was like, we’re going to die," Tessa Springer said. The couple said that once they landed, they evacuated the plane by jumping from its wing, with fellow passengers helping catch one another as they made their way to the ground. "I don’t think I’ll ever be able to get on another airplane ever again," Mark Springer said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Despite the frightening ordeal, Leff of "View from the Wing" said a lengthy delay due to a mechanical issue does not necessarily indicate that a flight is unsafe. "Part of that delay is diagnosing, part of it's addressing it and part of it's getting all the paperwork right and just doing all the final readbacks and rechecks to make sure that everything is safe for departure," Leff said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "A long delay in and of itself is not a safety concern," he added. Leff also noted that aircraft are equipped with multiple safety systems and emergency procedures designed to protect passengers when problems arise. "There are tremendous redundancies of systems and emergency procedures in place, such that the cockpit crew immediately reacted, responded and got everyone on the ground and off the aircraft to safety," Leff said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's certainly not something that you want to go through — but even when something goes wrong, that doesn't mean that things end badly at all," he added.

articles.title: Want flying cars? America needs thousands more Elon Musks and less red tape
articles.summary: Tesla's Roadster demonstration showed a car hovering in midair, but the real debate is why America needs 16,000 more Elon Musks to push boundaries.
articles.body: One of my favorite cartoons growing up was "The Jetsons." The Jetsons were a futuristic family living among the clouds with a fully automated life, from a robot maid named Rosie to technology that could make your dinner or do your laundry in just a few seconds at the push of a button. Everyone’s favorite aspect of this futuristic cartoon lifestyle boiled down to one element, which has become somewhat of a benchmark for technological progress: flying cars. And with Tesla’s recent exhibition, we are one step closer to that Jetsons-esque reality. If you haven’t seen the video, Tesla did a demonstration of their forthcoming Roadster vehicle, slated for 2028 production. The car swooped up a half-loop ramp reminiscent of Matchbox car stunts. At the top of the ramp, the car, which was upside down at the top, flipped over in midair. Then, thrusters seemed to suspend the car in midair, before helping guide it gently back down to land on the ground. For just a few moments, that car flew, and it was truly awe-inspiring. FLYING SPORTS CAR HIDES ITS WINGS AS PRODUCTION GETS CLOSER The reactions to this engineering feat and demonstration spectacle are somewhat of a Rorschach test. Those who love building, progress, technology or who are just generally optimistic have seen this demonstration as a formidable, impressive achievement. Those who like to see things torn down or are generally naysayers or obstacle formers react with "it’s not that big of a deal" or give other criticisms. Fortunately, America still has enough people committed to the entrepreneurial spirit to attract the likes of Elon Musk and provide a good home base for his talented team members and others who want to see Musk, America and human beings in general succeed. It isn’t hyperbole to say that Elon Musk is one of, if not the greatest, entrepreneurs of modern times. Regardless of any personal feelings or thoughts about Musk, if you can separate the art from the artist, or in his case, the entrepreneur from his business accomplishments, objectively, Musk has done the unthinkable time and time again. And we, as a country, are better off for him doing it from America as his home base. As my husband and I talked about Musk’s varying accomplishments, from his early work in online payments to his achievements in electric vehicle manufacturing and AI, to his SpaceX being able to catch rocket boosters returning to the Earth from outer space upon landing, and now this latest hovering automobile. We discussed that Musk reportedly held discussions with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company regarding a potential collaboration for his "Terafab" semiconductor facility in Texas. I mentioned that chip buildout had faced major challenges elsewhere, and my husband pointed out that it is different under Musk, saying, "In fact, we need 16,000 more Elon Musks." INNOVATION IS KEY TO AMERICA STAYING A SUPERPOWER. BUT IT IS MISSING AN ESSENTIAL PIECE And he’s right. America needs more Elon Musks. No, Elon Musk does not succeed on his own. There are many team members alongside him in undertaking outrageous projects and often making them succeed. But there’s something about Musk’s vision, leadership, hiring and willingness to inspire confidence in others, both on his team and in the general public, that makes his teams continue to be successful. And we need more of that. We need to not only attract and inspire those who may even be just a little bit like Musk, to dream bigger and bolder, to take calculated risks and try and try again when things don’t work the first time. And we need to make sure that we incentivize that behavior, instead of trying to penalize it or throw up roadblocks. THE NEXT AMERICAN BOOM COULD BE HERE — UNLESS WASHINGTON REGULATES IT TO DEATH In our own government, which is supposed to help vs. hinder entrepreneurs, we have politicians like Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is noted for going after Elon Musk because of his success, instead of trying to figure out a way to foster more Musk-like successes. After a vastly-ridiculed post made earlier this week from Warren lamenting, of all things, a possible merger between companies that make various spices and condiments, Mike Solana, CMO of Founders Fund and EIC of Pirate Wires, posted on X (also owned by Musk), highlighting the stark differences between the politician Warren and the creator Musk. His post said, "liz warren: we’re gonna stop the mayonnaise company from buying a hot sauce company." He then said, "elon musk:," and included the video from Musk of the Roadster’s hovering feat, perfectly illustrating how some in our country are erecting barriers and others are breaking barriers. America was founded on an idea of individual rights and incentives that rewarded successful pursuits, with such rewards growing at scale. We are very fortunate that we have Elon Musk and others who are pushing boundaries, bringing us into new frontiers, allowing Americans who work for him, who invest with him and who use his products or services to benefit alongside of him. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We do need 16,000 more Elon Musks. And the way to foster more Elon Musks is to appreciate, incentivize and reward entrepreneurship.

articles.title: Elderly Miss man killed with own gun in random home invasion as sheriff questions possible religious motive
articles.summary: A video captured the alleged burglar screaming what sounds like "God is dead" before the fatal home invasion that killed Bobby McGill in Mississippi.
articles.body: An elderly Mississippi man was fatally shot with his own gun while fighting an alleged burglar inside his home, and his wife managed to escape, authorities said. Union County Sheriff Jimmy Edwards told Fox News Digital that Eric Basco broke into Bobby McGill’s home around 4 a.m. Thursday while McGill and his wife were asleep. McGill, 81, struggled with Basco, who got hold of McGill’s gun and fatally shot him multiple times, Edwards said. MISSISSIPPI TEEN ALLEGEDLY KILLED ELDERLY COUPLE IN THEIR HOME BEFORE FIRING ON DEPUTIES IN STANDOFF "It appears that there was a struggle that had ensued between the assailant and the homeowner. And he had a pistol that he kept in his chest there at the foot of his bed," Edwards said. "It looks like to us that what we're piecing together, is that he may have tried to get that pistol and the individual was fighting him, and they had a fight and the guy got the pistol and shot Mr. Bobby multiple times." McGill's wife, Peggy, was able to escape the home safely and called 911 to report that someone "came into their house and attacked her husband," Edwards said. SUSPECT IN PITTSBURGH DOCTOR'S MURDER HAD BEEN RELEASED WITHOUT BAIL ON PRIOR BURGLARY CHARGE: COURT DOCS Edwards said Basco's likely motive was burglary, adding that he went into a bathroom and shot himself. Basco has since died at a hospital. However, Edwards said investigators obtained a video from the evening before the shooting that appears to show Basco walking down a road about 1.5 miles from McGill’s home, throwing his hands in the air and screaming what sounds like "God is dead." FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "It sounds like on the video that we saw that he was saying, ‘God is dead.’ Now, like I said, we're not 100% sure of that, but it sounds like that's what he was sayin'," Edwards said. "And in Mr. Bobby's yard was a cross and a sign that said, 'Jesus is Lord.' So did that help lure him to that house? I don't know. I'm not saying it did. I'm not saying it had anything at all to do with it. But it's a question that I have in my head if that played a part or not. I don't know, we'll probably never know." SEND US A TIP "It was a very sad, tragic thing, just for no reason," Edwards added. articles.title: Bronkhorstspruit water crisis in South Africa: 400 fall sick near Tshwane
articles.summary: More than 400 people, mostly children, become ill after drinking contaminated water, east of Pretoria.
articles.body:
Residents living near South Africa's capital, Pretoria, have been warned not to drink or cook with tap water after more than 400 people, mostly children under four, fell ill after drinking contaminated water.

The cases were detected in Tshwane, the area which includes Pretoria, after people reported to their local hospital with "stomach cramps and diarrhoea" over a two-week period, officials said.

No deaths have been reported but high levels of E. coli were found in the water.

Tshwane has faced numerous outbreaks from waterborne diseases in recent years. In 2023, 29 people were killed by a cholera outbreak in a township just outside Pretoria.

That outbreak, in Hammanskraal, was linked to substandard water purification practices.

In 2025, officials confirmed 48 cases of typhoid in the same area east of Pretoria. The source of the outbreak remains unclear.

No cholera bacteria has been found in the latest cases.

The departments of water and health, in a joint statement on Monday, said 408 cases had been detected between 7 and 18 October in about five townships.

They said that lab tests "indicate that the illness has been caused by residents being exposed to contaminated water" from a local water treatment facility supplying water to several communities east of Pretoria.

Samples tested found norovirus, campylobacter, shigella and "other pathogens that cause stomach cramps and diarrhoea", officials said.

The team's early investigations found that local authorities had failed to warn residents about the contaminated water.

The water supplied to the area has been declared unfit for human consumption and authorities urged residents to only use it to flush toilets. Tankers have been dispatched to supply clean drinking water.

"Previously stored water should be discarded, and water containers must be disinfected using household bleach," officials said.

articles.title: Influencer-model Shraddha Dubey, her sister arrested in UP businessman Shiva Sharma death case
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: Social media influencer and model Shraddha Dubey, her sister Rashmi Dubey and their driver, Tanveer Ali alias Danish, have been arrested in
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Social media influencer and model Shraddha Dubey, her sister Rashmi Dubey and their driver, Tanveer Ali alias Danish, have been arrested in Nagpur in connection with the death of restaurant owner Shiva Sharma, Lucknow Police Commissioner Tarun Gauba said.The three had been absconding and were reportedly carrying a combined reward of Rs 50,000. Gauba said they were being brought to Lucknow on transit remand and would be produced in court.The arrests followed a search across several locations in India and Nepal.Investigators tracked the accused after they reportedly fled to Nepal, returned to Uttar Pradesh and travelled to Nagpur in Maharashtra.Sharma, 28, died on October 9 after falling from the fourth floor of Awadh Green Apartments near Balu Adda in Lucknow’s Hazratganj area. His mother, Ranjana Sharma, accused Shraddha and others of being involved in his death. An FIR was registered on October 10 under Section 103(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which pertains to murder.Search across India-Nepal borderDuring the investigation, police found that the three accused had reportedly fled to Nepal. Shraddha’s SUV was found parked in Rupaidiha in Bahraich, near the India-Nepal border, raising suspicions that they had crossed into the neighbouring country.Investigators received further leads about their movements in Nepal, including in Banke and Surkhet. Later information placed them in Bhaluwang, in Dang district.Police also coordinated with their Nepalese counterparts to establish their whereabouts.The trio subsequently re-entered Uttar Pradesh through the Maharajganj border region, investigators found. They later travelled to Maharashtra, with Nagpur emerging as a key location in the search.The operation involved coordination between the Lucknow Police, the Uttar Pradesh Police Special Task Force (STF) and police personnel in Maharashtra. The joint teams eventually arrested the three in Nagpur.The Lucknow Police had earlier announced a reward of Rs 25,000 each for Shraddha, Rashmi and Danish, which would amount to Rs 75,000 in total. However, information about their arrest put the combined reward at Rs 50,000. The discrepancy requires official clarification.The case drew public attention after videos purportedly showing confrontations between Sharma and Shraddha surfaced.Shraddha had earlier denied involvement in his death in social media posts and claimed that Sharma died by suicide amid financial difficulties. articles.title: £30 rise in payments for crisis-hit Sheffield households
articles.summary: More money is made available through a resilience fund for hard-pressed households in Sheffield.
articles.body:
Crisis payments for people in Sheffield who are facing severe financial difficulties have been raised by £30.

Single person households which qualify for help from Sheffield City Council's crisis and resilience fund will now be entitled to a one-off payment of £95, up from £65 previously.

Meanwhile, two-person households can apply for a payment of £110, while homes with three or four people are entitled to £120 if they qualify and households with five or more people can get £130, the authority confirmed.

Announcing the change, councillor Elle Dodd, chair of the authority's finance and performance policy committee, said life was "difficult and expensive" for "too many people" in Sheffield.

The fund can be used to help people buy essentials such as food, toiletries and utilities, the council's website stated.

The increase was put in place after a cost-of-living review conducted by the committee, which is made up of a group of Sheffield councillors.

At least 7,000 crisis grants, totalling nearly £600,000, have already been awarded by the council since April.

Dodd said: "Behind every statistic is someone making impossible decisions, feeling stressed and looking for a little breathing room.

"We are determined to tackle the root causes of poverty, and to provide immediate support to those who need it.

"We are keeping tackling poverty and the cost of living firmly on the agenda."

articles.title: Match Preview: BVB Travel to Baku
articles.summary: It’s another UCL night (evening-ish)! BVB face off against Sabah this evening, travelling to Azerbaijan. If you’re anything like me, you’re probably wonderin...
articles.body:
BVB face off against Sabah this evening, travelling to Azerbaijan. If you're anything like me, you're probably wondering why a team from Azerbaijan is playing in a tournament run by UEFA, the European footballing body. If you're like me, you should also go look it up, because apparently a small part of Azerbaijan is indeed in Europe! I did not know that. Welcome then, Sabah, to the UCL!

Sabah FC have played in the Azerbaijani top flight since the 2018-2019 season, having been formally created as an organization is September of 2017. They played one season in the second division, and were promoted at the end of that season due to financial and licensing mistakes made by the top flight teams, as described by ESPN here . Now, after a few seasons, they have won the Azerbaijani league, and made it through the UCL knockouts to make their first appearance in Europe's premier footballing tournament.

Dortmund on the other hand are a team from Germany that play in yellow shirts. They are coming off the back of two league draws and a loss the Bodo/Glimt in the UCL. Not a great string of results for a team that started their season with five games undefeated. They will be looking to rebound their form against Sabah and steady the ship.

Given the team's recent results, expect Niko Kovac to make no changes. That is his usual approach to a bad string of results—double down. Maybe we will see Joey Veerman come in, as Dortmund should expect to have lots of the ball.

I'm not sure here. If you couldn't tell, I do not know much about Sabah, but I do know Dortmund. I know that Dortmund's attack is stuttering, and Kovac doesn't seem to be making any tactical tweaks to fix it. If Sabah hunker down and make attacking difficult for Dortmund, we could be in for another 0-0 or 1-1.

articles.title: Man charged with attack on Australian MP as suspect's father says she is family friend
articles.summary: Brendan Nugent's family say they have known Helen Haines, who remains in a critical condition, for more than 20 years.
articles.body:
A 43-year-old man has been charged after Australian MP Helen Haines was hit by a car in Victoria state on Monday.

The suspect will appear in court on Wednesday to face charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official.

Local media earlier named the alleged attacker as environmental activist Brendan Nugent. His father and his partner said they had been friends with Haines "for more than 20 years" and thanked residents and officers who helped her after the "shocking and horrific crime".

Haines remains in a critical condition after surgery and is reported to have lost one of her legs.

"Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community," Rod Nugent and his partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement.

"All of our love and all of our thoughts are with Helen and her family and friends."

They promised to assist Victoria Police "in any way we can".

Police say they will allege the incident was targeted.

Haines, 65, the independent member for Indi, is in a critical but stable condition after undergoing surgery at a Melbourne hospital.

'Our worst nightmare': Threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car

Shock and disbelief: How the attack on an Australian MP unfolded

What we know about Australian MP hit by car in apparent deliberate attack

She was airlifted there after bystanders rushed to help as the suspect allegedly struck her twice outside her office in Wangaratta.

The driver reportedly did a U-turn to get into position before hitting her, then reversed and hit her again, the home affairs minister told national broadcaster ABC.

She was pinned between two cars and later lost a leg, the ABC reports. The outlet also says doctors are fighting to save her other leg.

A local barber says he pulled the suspect out of his car and took a knife from him.

"I just wasn't comfortable with his movements so I took it out of his pocket and threw it away," Ricky Jefferies told reporters.

"I don't think I'm a hero. I think that I was just a person who had an opportunity to intervene in a safe-ish way."

Others who helped "didn't even check for danger," Jefferies said. "The car was still on and they sat in front of a rolling car, that's not an exaggeration."

In their statement, Victoria Police say a highway patrol unit was nearby at the time of the incident and "on scene" within eight seconds of the call coming through.

As they announced the charges against the 43-year-old, they said they had searched a property in Tarawingee, nearly 60km (40 miles) from Wangaratta.

"At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter," they said, adding officers would maintain a presence in Wangaratta.

Haines won the seat of Indi as an independent in 2019, and has since become a prominent member of the crossbench, building rapport across Australia's increasingly divided political spectrum.

Her office is on Wangaratta's main street, which reopened to traffic on Tuesday. Cars slowly filed past the growing number of bouquets being left for her on the pavement.

The community, and country, remain in shock.

At the vigil earlier on Tuesday, locals queued patiently in the cathedral aisle, waiting for their turn to light a candle. Priests hugged some of those who'd come to pay their respects.

On the pavement outside her office there were a growing number of bouquets being left for her.

One card read "may you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world".
